A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
A.q: A 32-year-old woman with long-standing asthma has had repeated exacerbations this year despite confirmed adherence and good inhaler technique. Her clinician suspects a hypersensitivity reaction to a mold. Which result supports that suspicion?
opts: Negative skin tests with a normal immunoglobulin E

Negative skin tests with a normal immunoglobulin E define intrinsic asthma, the non-allergic form. Tell: an Aspergillus hypersensitivity shows the opposite, a vigorous immunoglobulin E and G response to the mold.
A raised exhaled nitric oxide by itself

Fractional nitric oxide identifies airway inflammation, which any active asthma can show, so on its own it does not point to a mold. Tell: the specific finding is a vigorous antibody response to Aspergillus.
Raised immunoglobulin E and G to Aspergillus

Correct. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus seen almost exclusively in asthma or cystic fibrosis. Exposure causes a vigorous immunoglobulin E and G response that leads to acute symptoms and exacerbations, as in this woman.
Normal antibody levels argue against a hypersensitivity to the mold. Tell: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis produces a vigorous immunoglobulin E and G response to Aspergillus fumigatus.

A.io: Identify mechanisms for maintaining acid-base homeostasis.
A.q: What happens to carbon dioxide when ventilation increases?
opts: Carbon dioxide is not converted away here: increased ventilation removes carbon dioxide from the body, lowering it. Tell: ventilation clears carbon dioxide; the kidneys compensate for respiratory disorders by retaining or excreting bicarbonate.

Correct. Increased ventilation decreases carbon dioxide, and decreased ventilation increases it. In the steady state, carbon dioxide production matches excretion, so changing ventilation shifts the balance.
Carbon dioxide rises with decreased ventilation, not increased. More ventilation blows it off, so it falls. Tell: more breaths mean more carbon dioxide leaves, fewer breaths mean it builds up.

Ventilation changes carbon dioxide directly; the steady state, with production matching excretion, holds only while ventilation stays constant. Increasing ventilation raises excretion, so carbon dioxide falls. Tell: when excretion exceeds production, the level cannot stay the same.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for respiratory infections in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
A.q: A 74-year-old woman with acute bronchitis takes acetaminophen every day for knee osteoarthritis and wants a multisymptom cough and cold product for nighttime. Which counseling point is most important?
opts: Correct. Combination products are reviewed for their ingredients to prevent duplicate acetaminophen or other drugs, and she already takes acetaminophen daily. Sedation, interactions and comorbidities are discussed before any cough or cold product is recommended, which matters more at her age.
Pick one with codeine for sleep

Codeine-containing combinations are avoided routinely: limited benefit with sedation, respiratory depression and misuse risks. Using one as a sleep aid adds those risks in an older adult. Tell: the counseling goal is safety, not stronger cough suppression.
The product will shorten the illness

Short-term over-the-counter therapy offers limited benefit and does not shorten the illness. Promising otherwise sets a false expectation. Tell: these products relieve symptoms at best; the bronchitis runs its course either way.
Add an antibiotic if sputum yellows

Purulent or colored sputum does not establish bacterial infection and does not justify antibiotics. Tell: sputum color is not a reason to start an antibiotic, so it is not a counseling point to give her.

A.q: A 60-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and few symptoms asks to be started on an inhaled corticosteroid by itself because a friend with asthma uses one. Which regimen should be avoided in him?
opts: A single bronchodilator is the appropriate start for group A, few symptoms and low risk. Tell: it suits him; the regimen to avoid is a steroid inhaler used by itself.
Every patient should get the yearly influenza vaccine, which reduces hospitalizations and death. Tell: vaccination fits him; an inhaled corticosteroid alone is the regimen to avoid.

Correct. In this disease, inhaled corticosteroids must be combined with a long-acting beta agonist, and then with a long-acting antimuscarinic as triple therapy, and cannot be used on their own. They also raise pneumonia risk. Alone, they are an asthma treatment.
Smoking cessation is essential for every group and carries a survival benefit. Tell: it belongs in his plan; the steroid alone does not.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
A.q: A 34-year-old woman who works in a setting with ongoing tuberculosis transmission has a positive interferon-gamma release assay on targeted testing. She has no symptoms, her examination is normal and her chest radiograph is normal. Which best describes her tuberculosis status?
opts: Reactivation is latent infection that has progressed to disease, often with impaired immunity, so it brings symptoms or imaging findings. Tell: nothing here has progressed; she is still at the latent stage.

Progressive primary tuberculosis is disease that develops soon after initial infection when immune containment fails, so it brings clinical findings. Tell: a symptom-free woman with a normal examination and radiograph has contained infection, not progressive disease.

Disease needs more than an immune response: symptoms such as persistent cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss, or suspicious imaging, then microbiologic testing. Tell: she has none of these, and the blood test cannot by itself distinguish latent infection from disease.

Correct. A positive interferon-gamma release assay shows infection, and her clinical evaluation found no evidence of disease: no symptoms, a normal examination and a normal radiograph, which is usual in latent infection. Latent infection is asymptomatic and not infectious.

A.io: Identify mechanisms for maintaining acid-base homeostasis.
A.q: A 57-year-old man with severe obesity and a high fever from pneumonia has a carbon dioxide of 62 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg). What usually causes a raised carbon dioxide like his?
opts: Excess bicarbonate retained by the kidneys
Retained bicarbonate is compensation for a raised carbon dioxide; it does not raise the carbon dioxide itself. Tell: carbon dioxide is set by ventilation, bicarbonate by the kidneys.
Fever increases carbon dioxide production, but hypercapnia is usually from under-excretion, not excess production; normal breathing clears the extra. Tell: blame the breathing first.

Correct. Hypercapnia is usually the result of under-excretion (hypoventilation), not excess production. At steady state carbon dioxide production matches excretion, so a high level means ventilation is not keeping up.
Hyperventilation increases excretion and lowers carbon dioxide (hypocapnia). His is raised. Tell: hypercapnia is under-breathing, hypocapnia over-breathing.

A.q: A 38-year-old man with untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection has 3 weeks of progressive shortness of breath on exertion, a nonproductive cough, fever and weight loss. His respiratory rate is 28/min, and his lungs sound nearly normal. A chest radiograph shows diffuse bilateral infiltrates spreading out from the perihilar regions. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Lobar pneumococcal pneumonia gives an acute illness with purulent sputum and a dense consolidation confined to one lobe, with crackles and dullness over it. His cough is dry, his lungs are quiet and his infiltrates are bilateral. Tell: perihilar and bilateral is the Pneumocystis film, not a lobar one.

Mycoplasma is on the Pneumocystis differential, but it mostly affects school-age children and young adults in household or group outbreaks with gradual fever and a persistent cough. Tell: weeks of progressive exertional dyspnea in untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection point to the opportunistic fungus.

Correct. Untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection is the leading risk, and Pneumocystis is the most common opportunistic infection in that group. Progressive exertional dyspnea, a nonproductive cough, fever, a near-normal lung examination and diffuse bilateral perihilar infiltrates are its pattern.

Acute histoplasmosis follows inhaled soil or bird or bat droppings, with high fever, chills, myalgias, chest pain and headache 3 to 17 days after the exposure. No exposure is described. Tell: his story is defined by his immune status, not by an exposure history.

A.q: Recent hotel or cruise ship travel raises concern for which pneumonia pathogen?
opts: Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) is linked with exposure to farm animals or parturient cats. Tell: travel on a cruise ship or stay in a hotel points to Legionella.

Blastomyces dermatitidis is linked with travel to or residence in southeastern and south-central states bordering the Mississippi and Ohio River basins. Tell: hotel or cruise ship exposure points to Legionella.
Histoplasma capsulatum comes from soil with bat or bird droppings, mainly in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys. Tell: water droplets in hotels and cruise ships point to Legionella.

Correct. Hotel or cruise ship travel in the past two weeks is linked with Legionella species, which favors confined spaces and areas with circulating water droplets such as hot tubs or fountains. Legionella is one of the atypical pathogens.

A.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
A.q: A 37-year-old woman with asthma records her peak flow at home. Over the past week her morning readings before albuterol have been about 280 L/min and her afternoon readings after albuterol about 380 L/min. What does this pattern indicate?
opts: Correct. Peak flow is measured in the morning before and the afternoon after the bronchodilator, and a 20% change between them, or day to day, indicates poor control. A rise from 280 to 380 is about 36% of the morning value (26% of the afternoon value), well over the 20% line.
Normal circadian variation needing no action

Bronchial reactivity does vary through the day, but a swing of more than 20% between morning and afternoon is defined as poor control and needs review. Tell: the 20% threshold separates expected variation from poor control.
Good control would keep morning-to-afternoon variation under 20%. Her readings swing by about 36%. Tell: a large morning-to-afternoon gap is the hallmark of poor control, not good control.

A consistent pattern every morning and afternoon for a week, with higher readings after albuterol, fits real airway variation, not a broken device. Tell: the readings rise exactly when the bronchodilator works.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
A.q: Which medications act as asthma triggers and should be avoided in patients with asthma?
opts: These are controller medications that reduce inflammation or block leukotrienes, not triggers. The medications to avoid are aspirin and beta blockers. Tell: controllers prevent attacks; triggers provoke them.

Correct. Aspirin and beta blockers are the medication triggers listed and should be avoided in patients with asthma; exercise is listed with them as a trigger. Patients with true aspirin sensitivity should also avoid non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs.

These selective anti-inflammatory drugs may be used even in aspirin-sensitive asthma, so they are the safe alternatives. The triggers to avoid are aspirin and beta blockers. Tell: selective agents are what aspirin-sensitive patients switch to.

These are short-acting beta-2 agonists that relax airway smooth muscle and relieve symptoms. Aspirin and beta blockers are the medication triggers. Tell: an agonist at the beta-2 receptor opens the airway, while a beta blocker can close it.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
A.q: The clinical definition of chronic bronchitis requires chronic cough and sputum production for at least how long?
opts: One month in a single year is far short of the definition, which needs at least 3 months a year for 2 consecutive years. Tell: the definition is built on persistence across 2 years, not a single bout of cough.
3 months a year for 2 consecutive years

Correct. Chronic bronchitis is a clinical definition: chronic cough and sputum production typically for at least 3 months a year for 2 consecutive years. Emphysema, by contrast, is defined anatomically, by destruction and enlargement of the alveoli.
6 months a year for 3 consecutive years
Six months a year for 3 years overstates the threshold; the clinical definition is at least 3 months a year for 2 consecutive years. Tell: the numbers to remember are 3 and 2.
12 months a year for 5 consecutive years
Continuous cough for 5 years would qualify, but the definition is met far earlier, at 3 months a year for 2 consecutive years. Tell: the threshold is the minimum of 3 months over 2 years.

A.io: Explain how acid-base disorders affect electrolytes and oxygenation.
A.q: A 50-year-old woman with a metabolic alkalosis from repeated vomiting has generalized weakness and hyporeflexia. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.52 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 48 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 38 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which laboratory finding best explains her weakness and hyporeflexia?
opts: Hyperkalemia accompanies acidosis, as potassium shifts out of cells. Her pH is 7.52, and alkalosis shifts potassium into cells. Tell: alkalosis means low potassium.
Her bicarbonate is 38, high, which is what defines her metabolic alkalosis. A low bicarbonate belongs to metabolic acidosis. Tell: read her bicarbonate before choosing.

Her mildly raised carbon dioxide of 48 is compensation for the alkalosis; severe hypercapnia causes somnolence and confusion, not hyporeflexia. Tell: the weakness of metabolic alkalosis comes from potassium.
Correct. Metabolic alkalosis brings hypokalemia (potassium shifts into cells, and vomiting adds losses), and the associated hypokalemia causes weakness and hyporeflexia. Her alkalemia at 7.52 fits.

A.q: A 59-year-old man has been intubated and mechanically ventilated for 3 days after a motor vehicle crash. He develops a new fever, purulent endotracheal secretions and a new infiltrate. How should this pneumonia be classified?
opts: Hospital-acquired pneumonia is pneumonia 48 hours or more after admission; when it follows more than 48 hours of endotracheal intubation, the specific label is ventilator associated. Tell: the breathing tube decides the name.

The health care-associated category is retired and is no longer used to classify pneumonia or choose therapy. Tell: the current labels are community acquired, hospital acquired and ventilator associated, decided by setting and timing.

Community-acquired pneumonia is acquired outside the hospital or present early in admission. His began after 3 days on the ventilator. Tell: an infection that starts after more than 48 hours of intubation is not community acquired.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Ventilator-associated pneumonia develops more than 48 hours after endotracheal intubation, and he has been ventilated for 3 days. Colonized secretions inhaled through the tube cause it, and it carries higher mortality and a longer intensive care stay.

A.io: Identify and discuss vaccines which prevent respiratory infections.
A.q: A 72-year-old man with no immune problems received the updated 2026-2027 coronavirus disease 2019 vaccine in September. He asks whether he needs anything more this season. Which plan is appropriate?
opts: A second dose about 6 months later

Correct. An updated 2026-2027 vaccine is recommended for adults 18 or older, and adults 65 or older generally need two seasonal doses about 6 months apart. At 72 he needs a second dose about 6 months after September.
One seasonal dose fits adults younger than 65 without immunocompromise. At 72 he generally needs two seasonal doses about 6 months apart. Tell: age 65 or older adds the second dose.

The seasonal second dose for adults 65 or older comes about 6 months after the first, not after 4 weeks. Tell: a 4-week interval is the influenza two-dose spacing for young children, not this schedule.
Adults 65 or older generally need two seasonal doses about 6 months apart, not monthly doses. Tell: the schedule is two doses per season for his age group.

A.q: A 58-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is ready to quit smoking and asks for a medicine to help. He has tried quitting alone twice. Which plan is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Every smoking cessation attempt should be combined with counseling, which looks for triggers and gives coping strategies, to increase efficacy. Varenicline, bupropion or nicotine replacement can be added; his failed solo attempts make the combined plan the better choice.
Varenicline is a listed cessation aid, but all attempts should be combined with counseling to increase efficacy. Tell: he has already failed alone twice; behavioral support is the missing piece.
Cutting down without a quit date
Smoking cessation carries a survival benefit, so cutting down is not the goal. Tell: a structured quit attempt with counseling and medicine is the listed approach.

Tiotropium is a long-acting antimuscarinic bronchodilator with mainly dry mouth as a side effect; it does nothing for nicotine dependence. Tell: the medicines that aid quitting are varenicline, bupropion and nicotine replacement.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
A.q: A 72-year-old woman with asthma, already on an inhaled corticosteroid and a long-acting beta-2 agonist, has heart disease and worries about side effects. Her clinician is considering adding tiotropium. Which property of tiotropium is reassuring for her?
opts: Correct. Tiotropium, an anticholinergic, has little or no systemic absorption and therefore few side effects. It inhibits only the cholinergic reflex part of bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion, and it is less effective than beta-2 agonists with a slow onset.

Anticholinergics are less effective than beta-2 agonists because they block only the cholinergic component of bronchoconstriction. Tell: its advantage is safety, from little systemic absorption, not strength.

Tiotropium inhibits the cholinergic reflex component of bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion; it is not an anti-inflammatory controller. Tell: anti-inflammatory control comes from her inhaled corticosteroid.
Fast onset that suits rescue use
Tiotropium has a slow onset of action, so it is not a rescue medicine. Tell: her rescue medicine stays the short-acting beta-2 agonist; tiotropium's appeal for her is its low side-effect burden.

A.io: Explain how acid-base disorders affect electrolytes and oxygenation.
A.q: In acidosis, what happens to oxygen delivery to the tissues?
opts: Decreased delivery is the alkalosis effect, caused by higher affinity. In acidosis, affinity falls and delivery increases. Tell: acid releases oxygen to tissues, alkali holds it back.

Correct. Acidosis decreases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen and shifts the dissociation curve to the right, so hemoglobin releases more oxygen to the tissues and oxygen delivery increases. Alkalosis does the reverse.
Delivery does not stop in acidosis. Hemoglobin lets go of oxygen more easily, so tissue delivery increases. Tell: the change is a shift in degree, not an all-or-none stop.
pH does change delivery. Acidosis lowers hemoglobin's affinity and increases oxygen delivery to the tissues. Tell: the acid-base state sets how tightly hemoglobin holds oxygen.

A.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
A.q: What does the modified Medical Research Council dyspnea scale grade?
opts: Exacerbation risk comes from the number of exacerbations and hospitalizations in the past year. Tell: the dyspnea scale measures day-to-day breathlessness.
Survival is estimated with the BODE (body mass index, obstruction, dyspnea, exercise) index, which uses the dyspnea grade as one input. Tell: the scale itself grades breathlessness.
Airflow obstruction is graded from the post-bronchodilator 1-second volume, grades 1 to 4. Tell: the dyspnea scale is a self-reported symptom grade, not a spirometric one.

Correct. The modified Medical Research Council scale grades breathlessness from 0 (breathless only with strenuous exercise) to 4 (too breathless to leave the house, or breathless dressing). A grade of 2 or more counts as more symptoms.

A.q: A 66-year-old woman being treated for community-acquired pneumonia becomes newly confused. Her heart rate is 118/min, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 87% on room air, and her urine output has fallen. Which complication has developed?
opts: Correct. When pneumonia becomes systemic it progresses toward bacteremia or septicemia: tachycardia with hypotension, hypoxia, confusion or altered mental status, and decreased urine output or kidney function. She has every one of those signs, which changes her site of care and urgency of support.

Empyema is suggested by dullness to percussion at the base of the lung, a local pleural complication that is drained when indicated. It does not by itself explain hypotension, confusion and falling urine output. Tell: her findings are systemic, not a local pleural sign.

A lung abscess develops insidiously over weeks with foul sputum, hemoptysis and a cavity with an air-fluid level. Her change is acute, with signs of circulatory collapse. Tell: abscess is slow and local; septicemia is fast and systemic.

Pleurisy is heard as a pleural rub, a local finding when the infection irritates the pleura. Her problem is circulatory failure with organ dysfunction. Tell: a rub is a chest sound; hypotension with confusion and low urine output is a systemic picture.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
A.q: A 17-year-old runner with exercise-induced bronchospasm uses albuterol before every practice, yet still has frequent symptoms during training. Which change is most likely to prevent his episodes?
opts: Cromolyn prevents symptoms but does not relieve them once present, so taking it during an episode does not help. Tell: the agent that best prevents exercise-induced bronchospasm is a regular inhaled corticosteroid.

Asthma treatment aims for no limitation on physical activity, so giving up running is not the goal. Tell: regular inhaled corticosteroid use best prevents exercise-induced bronchospasm and keeps him training.

Correct. Exercise-induced bronchospasm is treated with a short-acting beta-2 agonist before exercise but is best prevented with regular inhaled corticosteroid use. His frequent symptoms despite pre-exercise albuterol call for the regular controller.
Saving albuterol for after symptoms start

Albuterol helps most when used before exercise, and moving it to after symptoms begin gives up that protection. Tell: when pre-exercise albuterol is not enough, prevention comes from a regular inhaled corticosteroid.

A.q: A 20-year-old college student has had 10 days of gradual fever, a persistent cough and headache. Several students in her dormitory have the same illness, and a respiratory nucleic acid test is positive for Mycoplasma pneumoniae. She has taken amoxicillin for 3 days without improvement. Which change is most appropriate?
opts: Cefpodoxime is another beta-lactam, and beta-lactams are ineffective against Mycoplasma because it lacks a cell wall. Tell: change the drug class to a macrolide or doxycycline.

Adding clavulanate makes amoxicillin-clavulanate, still a beta-lactam. Mycoplasma has no cell wall for any beta-lactam to act on. Tell: the failure is a drug-class mismatch, not resistance that a beta-lactamase inhibitor could fix.

A longer course of an ineffective drug cannot help: Mycoplasma has no cell wall, so beta-lactams do not work at any duration. Tell: her lack of response is expected, and the fix is a macrolide or doxycycline.

Correct. Beta-lactams are ineffective against Mycoplasma because it lacks a cell wall, so amoxicillin cannot work. Adults with Mycoplasma infection are treated with a macrolide such as azithromycin or with doxycycline, and a respiratory fluoroquinolone is an alternative.

A.q: A 64-year-old woman with severe community-acquired pneumonia in the intensive care unit had methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus isolated from her sputum last year. She has been started on ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Which agent should be added?
opts: Correct. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus coverage is added only for validated risks, and a prior respiratory isolate is one. The agents named for it are vancomycin or linezolid, added to the beta-lactam combination; cultures are obtained and therapy de-escalated as results return.

Ertapenem is named as not a reliable antipseudomonal option and is not one of the agents listed for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Tell: her validated risk is the resistant staphylococcus, so the add-on is vancomycin or linezolid.

Clindamycin is held back even in lung abscess because of Clostridioides difficile risk, and it is not an agent listed for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia. Tell: the listed agents are vancomycin or linezolid.

Moxifloxacin is a respiratory fluoroquinolone that can partner a beta-lactam in severe pneumonia, but it is not a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus agent and is not reliable for Pseudomonas. Tell: the agents named for resistant staphylococcus are vancomycin or linezolid.

A.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
A.q: A 23-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has diabetic ketoacidosis with Kussmaul respirations (deep, rapid breathing). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.19 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 21 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 8 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which approach corrects her acid-base disorder?
opts: Correct. Elevated-gap metabolic acidosis is treated by treating the underlying disorder; her pH of 7.19 is acidemic but not in the unsustainable range below 6.7. Her deep breathing is compensation and is left alone.

Rebreathing would blunt her compensation, and a paper bag is not necessary even in hyperventilation, with only a placebo effect. Her acidosis is metabolic, and the cause is treated. Tell: a bag does not treat a metabolic acidosis.
Bicarbonate until her pH is normal

Therapy to normalize the pH may be warranted at unsustainable values (below 6.7), along with treatment of the cause. At 7.19 she needs the ketoacidosis treated. Tell: treat the cause; pH-directed therapy belongs to unsustainable values.
Slow her breathing to retain carbon dioxide
Her deep, rapid breathing is the compensation lowering carbon dioxide; slowing it would drop her pH further. Tell: compensatory hyperventilation is protective in metabolic acidosis.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
A.q: A 66-year-old woman is being discharged after a hospitalization for an exacerbation. Her blood eosinophil count is elevated. Which action belongs in her discharge bundle?
opts: Holding maintenance therapy raises the risk of another exacerbation. Tell: the bundle starts long-acting bronchodilators promptly, before she leaves. Prompt start is part of the bundle.
Pulmonary rehabilitation is considered as part of the discharge bundle, and it reduces readmissions. Tell: rehabilitation is planned at discharge, not put off for months.

Oral corticosteroids are for acute exacerbations only, not long-term use after discharge. Tell: maintenance after an admission is long-acting inhaled therapy, plus an inhaled steroid with high eosinophils.

Correct. The discharge bundle begins long-acting bronchodilators promptly, considers an inhaled corticosteroid if eosinophils are elevated (as hers are), checks inhaler technique, considers pulmonary rehabilitation, arranges follow-up and explains the recovery timeline.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
A.q: A 60-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 70% predicted, a 6-minute walk distance of 420 meters, a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 2, and a body mass index of 25. Based on her BODE (body mass index, obstruction, dyspnea, exercise) index, what is her estimated 4-year survival?
opts: About 18% belongs to scores of 7 to 10. Her total is only 1. Tell: only the dyspnea grade of 2 earns a point. Her walk distance of 420 meters and 1-second volume of 70% both score 0.
About 57% belongs to scores of 5 to 6. Her total is 1. Tell: a 1-second volume of 70% and a walk of 420 meters each score 0. Her body mass index of 25 scores 0 as well.
About 67% belongs to scores of 3 to 4. Her total is 1, from the dyspnea grade alone. Tell: 0 to 2 points predicts about 80%. She would need 2 more points to reach 3.

Correct. 1-second volume 70% (65 or more) = 0 + walk 420 meters (350 or more) = 0 + dyspnea grade 2 = 1 + body mass index 25 (over 21) = 0, for a total of 1. Scores of 0 to 2 predict about 80% 4-year survival.

A.io: Identify compensatory mechanisms for simple acid-base disorders.
A.q: A 30-year-old woman with a normal-gap metabolic acidosis from a ureteral diversion has a bicarbonate of 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). By the Winter formula, what carbon dioxide range is expected if she is compensating appropriately?
opts: 19 to 23 is 1.5 x 14 = 21, plus or minus 2, without adding the 8. The formula adds 8, giving 29 and a range of 27 to 31. Tell: the midpoint of the range is 29.
20 to 24 uses 1.0 instead of 1.5 times the bicarbonate (14 + 8 = 22). The formula is 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29, giving a range of 27 to 31. Tell: the multiplier is 1.5.
Correct. Winter formula: expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 21 + 8 = 29, plus or minus 2, so 27 to 31 mm Hg. The formula needs only the bicarbonate, whatever the anion gap is or its cause.
36 to 44 is the normal range, and in metabolic acidosis the lungs lower the carbon dioxide below it. Winter gives 27 to 31. Tell: expected carbon dioxide falls as bicarbonate falls.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
A.q: A 68-year-old woman taking theophylline for asthma has nausea, vomiting, headache and a rapid irregular heartbeat. Her potassium is low and her glucose high. Which explanation best fits her presentation?
opts: An aspirin-sensitive reaction brings rhinorrhea, conjunctival irritation, flushing and wheeze after aspirin, and aspirin is not part of her story. Tell: vomiting, arrhythmia, hypokalemia and hyperglycemia in a theophylline user point to toxicity.
ruled out by a stated finding

Inhaled corticosteroids cause local effects: hoarseness, cough and oral thrush. Their systemic side effects are minimal, so they do not explain vomiting, arrhythmia and low potassium. Tell: her systemic toxic picture belongs to the drug with a narrow toxic-therapeutic range, theophylline.

Muscle tremor and palpitations are the listed side effects of the short-acting beta-2 agonist class. Vomiting, headache and the arrhythmia with low potassium and high glucose are the listed toxic effects of theophylline, and the stem names theophylline. Tell: the whole cluster matches theophylline toxicity.

Correct. Theophylline has a narrow toxic-therapeutic range, and its toxic effects are nausea, vomiting, tachyarrhythmias, headache, seizure, hyperglycemia and hypokalemia, matching this woman's picture. That toxicity is why it is rarely used and needs close monitoring.

A.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
A.q: An 80-year-old man on home oxygen at 5 L/min by nasal cannula with no humidifier complains of a sore, dry nose and occasional bleeding. Which change addresses the cause?
opts: Correct. He is on 5 L/min by nasal cannula with no humidifier, and has a sore, dry nose with bleeding. That is mucosal irritation. Humidity is used with cannula flow rates greater than 4 L/min, so adding humidity to the oxygen treats the cause.
Raising the flow to 6 L/min keeps him above 4 L/min, where humidity is already needed and he has none. A higher flow leaves the missing humidity in place. Tell: fix the humidity, not the flow.

A non-rebreather mask is a high-fraction device for severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well. He has a sore nose, not worsening hypoxia, and the mask would not solve it. Tell: his problem is dryness at a flow above 4 L/min.
Apply a petroleum lip and nose balm

A petroleum-based balm is on the list of products to avoid with home oxygen, because oxygen is highly flammable. It would not be an appropriate treatment for his nose. Tell: petroleum products stay away from oxygen.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.io: Identify compensatory mechanisms for simple acid-base disorders.
A.q: A 40-year-old man has a pH of 7.30 (normal 7.35 to 7.45) and a carbon dioxide of 52 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg). To decide whether this respiratory problem is acute or chronic, which value is compared with its expected level?
opts: Correct. For a respiratory disorder, compensation is renal, so the expected bicarbonate is checked. A small rise (about 1 per 10 mm Hg) means acute, and a large rise (about 3.5 per 10) means chronic.
The anion gap sorts metabolic acidosis and says nothing about respiratory chronicity. The rise in bicarbonate does. Tell: the gap uses sodium, chloride and bicarbonate to type a metabolic disorder.
Urine chloride types a metabolic alkalosis. Respiratory chronicity is judged from the bicarbonate. Tell: the kidney's compensation for respiratory problems appears in serum bicarbonate.

The expected carbon dioxide is calculated for a metabolic disorder, as with the Winter formula. A respiratory disorder is checked by its bicarbonate. Tell: his carbon dioxide is the primary problem, so it is not the compensation check.

A.q: What risk of death does a CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or older) total of 2 carry?
opts: A risk of death under 3% belongs to a total of 0 to 1, low severity, usually treated at home unless there are other reasons for admission. Tell: 2 points is moderate severity, about 9%.

Correct. A total of 2 points is moderate severity, with a risk of death of about 9%, and the pathway sends these patients to the hospital. A total of 0 to 1 is low severity (under 3%), and 3 to 5 is high severity (15 to 40%).
A 15 to 40% risk belongs to a total of 3 to 5, high severity, with urgent senior review and consideration of critical care. Tell: 2 points is moderate, about 9%.
About 27% is the mortality of Pneumonia Severity Index class V, a different score. Tell: the five-item score at 2 points carries about 9%.

A.q: A 9-year-old boy has influenza with a temperature of 102.8°F and body aches. His parent wants to give him a fever medicine from the cabinet at home. Which medication should be avoided?
opts: Rest and hydration are the core of influenza supportive care, especially when fever and poor intake cause mild volume depletion. Tell: the measure to avoid is a drug, aspirin, not fluids.

Correct. Aspirin is avoided in children younger than 18 years with influenza because it is associated with Reye syndrome. Acetaminophen or ibuprofen is used for fever as part of supportive care, along with rest and fluids.

Acetaminophen is one of the listed antipyretics for influenza supportive care and is appropriate for a child. Tell: the antipyretic to avoid under 18 is aspirin, because of its association with Reye syndrome.

Ibuprofen is one of the listed antipyretics for influenza supportive care. Tell: the age warning applies to aspirin, which is avoided in anyone younger than 18 with influenza because of Reye syndrome.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
A.q: An 80-year-old woman with advanced chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, frequent admissions and declining function lives with her daughter, who helps with her care. She has not discussed her wishes for future care. Which step is most appropriate now?
opts: Wait for the final days of life
Delaying palliative care until the end loses the chance to plan with caregivers and set advance directives. Tell: in older adults it is integrated early.

Correct. For older adults, palliative care is integrated early, with caregiver involvement and advance directives, and priorities shift to function, quality of life, multimorbidity and goals of care. Her daughter's involvement makes it timely.
Focus on her returning to work
Returning to work is a rehabilitation aim for working-age adults. Tell: at 80 with advanced disease, the priorities are function, quality of life and goals of care.
Add triple therapy and recheck in a year
Medication changes may help, but they do not address her goals of care, and a year is a long gap for advanced disease. Tell: early palliative care with her daughter is the listed approach.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
A.q: A 34-year-old woman who works in a furniture-finishing plant has had cough and wheezing for 6 months. She notes the symptoms ease on weekends and nearly vanish during a 2-week vacation, then return within days of going back to work. She has no history of allergies. Which diagnosis best explains her pattern?
opts: Exercise-induced bronchospasm is triggered by exertion and clears soon after. Her symptoms persist through the work week and clear only away from work. Tell: the trigger is a place, not an activity.

Extrinsic asthma is atopic and allergen-triggered, and she has no allergy history. Tell: the weekly work-linked rhythm, with improvement away from the plant, is the occupational pattern, and occupational sensitization does not require atopy.
ruled out by a stated finding

Catamenial asthma follows the menstrual cycle, a monthly rhythm. Her symptoms follow her work schedule, easing on weekends and vacations. Tell: a weekly on-off pattern tied to the job points to the workplace, not to hormones.

Correct. Symptoms that improve on weekends and vacations and return at work point to occupational asthma from a workplace sensitizer, here chemicals in furniture finishing. Occupational sensitization is independent of atopy, so her lack of allergies does not argue against it.

Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
A.q: Which new symptom should prompt a patient with acute bronchitis to return for reassessment?
opts: Colored mucus can occur in bronchitis and does not differentiate viral from bacterial infection. Tell: sputum color is not a return precaution; coughing up blood is.

Correct. Return precautions for acute bronchitis are dyspnea, hemoptysis, persistent fever, hypoxemia, or worsening after initial improvement. Expected-course counseling and these explicit precautions are the safety net when antibiotics are withheld.

A cough commonly lasts 2 to 3 weeks in acute bronchitis, so a cough at 2 weeks is the expected course. Tell: the return triggers are dyspnea, hemoptysis, persistent fever, hypoxemia or worsening after improvement.

Chest tightness or substernal discomfort is one of the usual symptoms of acute bronchitis. Tell: return precautions are dyspnea, hemoptysis, persistent fever, hypoxemia or worsening after improvement.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
A.q: A 64-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is taught to breathe out slowly through pursed lips when she is short of breath. She asks why it helps. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Mucus hypersecretion comes from gland hyperplasia in chronic bronchitis and is not changed by breathing technique. Tell: pursed-lip breathing raises airway pressure to prevent collapse.
Pursed lips act during expiration, slowing outflow and raising airway pressure; they do not speed inspiration. Tell: the problem being treated is airway collapse while breathing out.

Correct. Pursed-lip breathing increases intra-airway pressure, which keeps the airways open during expiration and allows more gas exchange. It counters the collapse of airways that loss of elastic recoil causes in emphysema.

Pursed-lip breathing works on airway pressure, not on the heart; heart rate is often above 100 in these patients for other reasons. Tell: the benefit is mechanical, holding airways open during expiration.

A.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
A.q: A 34-year-old man is brought in after running a generator in a closed garage. He has a headache and is confused; pulse oximetry reads 98%. Which treatment is indicated?
opts: A nebulized bronchodilator delivers liquid medication to the airways, and nothing in his story suggests airway disease. His headache and confusion follow exposure to exhaust in a closed space. Tell: nebulizers treat airway problems; carbon monoxide poisoning is treated with oxygen.
No oxygen, since saturation is normal

A normal saturation does not rule out oxygen here, because carbon monoxide poisoning is itself a listed indication, along with hypoxia, perioperative needs, air hunger and cluster headache. Tell: when the indication is poisoning, the reading of 98% is not the deciding clue.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. After exposure to generator exhaust in a closed garage, his headache and confusion fit carbon monoxide poisoning, which is a listed indication for oxygen therapy. The normal reading of 98% does not remove that indication, so oxygen is the treatment.

Breathing into a paper bag is not a therapy for this exposure. Carbon monoxide poisoning is listed among the respiratory conditions for which oxygen therapy is indicated. Tell: the exhaust exposure in a closed garage calls for oxygen, not rebreathing.

A.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
A.q: A 26-year-old man is found unresponsive at a party with pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.24 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 62 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 26 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: Correct. The pH of 7.24 is acidemia, and the carbon dioxide of 62 is high, which matches it, so the problem is respiratory. Bicarbonate rose only about 1 per 10 mm Hg (22 above 40 gives about 26), the acute response. A slow rate of 6 fits central nervous system depression.

Respiratory alkalosis is a high pH from a low carbon dioxide. He has a pH of 7.24 and a carbon dioxide of 62, and both point the other way. Tell: check the pH first; 7.24 is acidemia, so no alkalosis is possible.

Chronic respiratory acidosis would show a much larger bicarbonate rise, about 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg, or near 32 here (22 mm Hg above 40). His 26 is the small acute rise. Tell: a bicarbonate near 26 means the kidneys have not had their 6 to 12 hours or more.

Metabolic acidosis needs a low bicarbonate driving the low pH, and his bicarbonate is 26, within normal. The raised carbon dioxide of 62 is the value that matches the acidemia. Tell: when bicarbonate is normal and carbon dioxide is high, the problem is respiratory.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.q: A 62-year-old man has coronavirus disease 2019 with fever and cough. His oxygen saturation is 91% on room air, his respiratory rate is 32/min, and imaging shows infiltrates over more than half of his lung volume. He is not in shock and does not need mechanical ventilation. Which severity category fits?
opts: Mild illness means some symptoms with no shortness of breath and a normal chest radiograph. He has hypoxemia, marked tachypnea and extensive infiltrates. Tell: any abnormal imaging already moves a patient past mild.
Moderate illness has a positive radiograph with an oxygen saturation of at least 94% on room air. His saturation is 91%. Tell: falling below 94% on room air is the line between moderate and severe.

Correct. Severe illness is an oxygen saturation below 94% on room air, marked tachypnea or infiltrates over more than 50% of the lung volume, and he has all three. Critical illness needs acute respiratory failure, septic shock or multiple organ dysfunction, which he does not have.

Critical illness means acute respiratory failure, septic shock or multiple organ dysfunction. He is not in shock and does not need ventilation. Tell: low oxygen and tachypnea without organ failure are severe, not critical.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
A.q: A 25-year-old woman with asthma wakes most nights at about 3 in the morning with cough and wheeze, though she feels fine in the daytime. She asks why her symptoms come at night. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Her rescue inhaler wears off at night
Her symptoms come at a fixed early-morning hour. Tell: the nightly timing follows a circadian peak in bronchial reactivity at 3 to 4 in the morning.
Night symptoms point to vocal fold dysfunction

Vocal fold dysfunction is an upper airway mimic; night waking with cough and wheeze is a typical asthma pattern. Tell: asthma may be worse at night because bronchial reactivity peaks at 3 to 4 in the morning.
Bronchial reactivity peaks in the early morning hours

Correct. Asthma symptoms may be worse at night because of circadian variation in bronchomotor tone and bronchial reactivity, which peaks around 3 to 4 in the morning, the time she wakes. Night waking also counts when classifying severity.
Cardiac asthma is wheezing from decompensated heart failure, and a healthy 25-year-old has no heart failure. Tell: her waking at 3 in the morning matches the circadian peak in bronchial reactivity.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
A.q: A 66-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease had 3 moderate exacerbations in the past year. Her blood eosinophil count is 110. She is starting maintenance therapy. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Adding an inhaled corticosteroid is considered in group E when eosinophils are 300 or more. Hers are 110. Tell: without that eosinophil count, the steroid's pneumonia risk is not justified.
Oral corticosteroids are for acute exacerbations only in this disease, not daily maintenance. Tell: exacerbation prevention comes from long-acting inhaled bronchodilators.

Correct. Three moderate exacerbations make her high risk, group E, which starts on a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic. Her eosinophil count of 110 is below 300, so an inhaled corticosteroid, with its pneumonia risk, is not added.
A single bronchodilator is the group A start, for low risk and few symptoms. Three exacerbations make her group E. Tell: high risk calls for both long-acting bronchodilators.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
A.q: A 45-year-old man's wife was diagnosed with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis last month. His tuberculin skin test, read at 72 hours, shows 7 mm of induration. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: 10 mm is the cut-off for increased exposure risk, selected medical risks, high-risk congregate settings and children under 5. Tell: living with a wife who has infectious tuberculosis is recent close contact, which drops his cut-off to 5 mm.
Negative until there is 10 mm of redness
Erythema is not measured; the trained reader measures transverse induration in millimeters. Tell: his 7 mm of induration is the value to compare with his 5 mm cut-off, whatever the redness.

Correct. A recent close contact belongs in the 5 mm group, with human immunodeficiency virus, transplant, major immunosuppression and imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis. 7 mm meets that cut-off, so he is positive and needs clinical evaluation and chest imaging before any preventive treatment.
15 mm is for people with no known tuberculosis risk factors. Tell: a household contact of an infectious case has a major exposure, so his cut-off is the lowest one, 5 mm.

A.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
A.q: Sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145), chloride 104 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106) and bicarbonate 12 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26). What is the calculated anion gap?
opts: 12 is the bicarbonate value itself, not the gap. The gap is 140 - (104 + 12) = 24. Tell: the answer comes from the subtraction, not a single listed value.

Correct. Anion gap = sodium - (chloride + bicarbonate) = 140 - (104 + 12) = 140 - 116 = 24. That is above the normal 9 to 15, so this is an elevated anion gap, as expected with such a low bicarbonate.
36 comes from 140 - 104 without subtracting the bicarbonate. The gap subtracts chloride and bicarbonate: 140 - 116 = 24. Tell: both anions are subtracted.
48 adds the bicarbonate instead of subtracting it (140 - 104 + 12). The correct arithmetic is 140 - (104 + 12) = 24. Tell: chloride and bicarbonate are added together first and the sum is subtracted.

Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
A.q: A 39-year-old man with no immune problems has a cough and a lung nodule, and his serum cryptococcal antigen is positive. A lumbar puncture is normal, and there is no sign of disseminated disease. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Mild isolated pulmonary cryptococcosis is treated with fluconazole, generally for 6 to 12 months. His normal lumbar puncture and lack of dissemination keep him out of the severe category that needs amphotericin B plus flucytosine induction.

Observation is the approach for mild acute histoplasmosis in a healthy adult. Mild isolated pulmonary cryptococcosis is still treated, with fluconazole. Tell: the observation option belongs to the other fungus.

Amphotericin B plus flucytosine induction is for severe pulmonary, central nervous system or disseminated disease. His lumbar puncture is normal and there is no dissemination. Tell: a normal lumbar puncture keeps him on the mild pathway.

Doxycycline is the preferred adult treatment for psittacosis, a bacterial infection from birds, and has no antifungal role. Tell: a positive cryptococcal antigen calls for an azole antifungal, fluconazole.

A.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
A.q: Besides being flammable, which property of oxygen tanks shapes the teaching about storage and disposal?
opts: Oxygen tanks are not described as expiring after one week. The stated property is that they contain compressed gas, and that is what drives storage and disposal teaching. Tell: the property concerns pressure, not a time limit.

Oxygen tanks do not contain a liquid fuel. They contain compressed gas, which is the property that shapes the teaching about proper storage and disposal. Tell: the key is a compressed gas, not a fuel.

Nothing in the teaching says oxygen tanks release carbon monoxide; the carbon monoxide alarms are a separate safety step, tested monthly. The property taught for tanks is that they contain compressed gas. Tell: the key describes how the tank holds oxygen.

Correct. Oxygen tanks contain compressed gas, in addition to oxygen being highly flammable, and that is why storage and disposal are taught. Tanks are stored and disposed of properly, not handled casually.

A.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
A.q: A 74-year-old man on home oxygen has a gas water heater with a pilot light in the hallway where he likes to sit. How far from it should his oxygen be kept?
opts: Two feet is far short of the stated distance. Oxygen is highly flammable, and the minimum from heat sources such as pilot lights is at least 10 feet. Tell: the distance in the teaching is 10, not 2.
Five feet is only half the stated minimum. The teaching specifies at least 10 feet from heat sources, and a pilot light is a flame. Tell: if the number is smaller than 10 feet, it is too close.

Correct. Home oxygen teaching is to keep oxygen at least 10 feet from heat sources, which include pilot lights, electric appliances and candles. A gas water heater with a pilot light sits in the hallway where he sits, so his oxygen must be kept at least 10 feet away.

Fifty feet is farther than the stated minimum, and it would be impractical inside a home. The teaching gives at least 10 feet from heat sources. Tell: the guideline is a minimum of 10 feet, not a vague large distance.

A.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
A.q: A 57-year-old man with confirmed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a symptom assessment test score of 7 and a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 1. He has had no exacerbations in the past year. Under the current three-group scheme, which group is he in?
opts: Correct. A symptom score of 7 (under 10) and a dyspnea grade of 1 (0 to 1) mean fewer symptoms, and no exacerbations means low risk. Low symptoms with low risk is group A, which starts with a single bronchodilator.
Group C belongs to the 2020 four-group scheme (few symptoms, high risk), and he is low risk anyway. Tell: the current scheme has only A, B and E. Without high risk, he cannot be C in either scheme.
Group B is low risk with more symptoms: a symptom score of 10 or more or a dyspnea grade of 2 or more. His 7 and grade 1 are below both. Tell: fewer symptoms keep him in A.
Group E is high risk: 2 or more moderate exacerbations or 1 hospitalization in the past year. He had none. Tell: without exacerbations, his group is set by symptoms alone.

A.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
A.q: A 50-year-old man has a metabolic alkalosis with a high urine chloride. He takes no diuretics and has not vomited. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 47 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 34 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which finding should be checked next to narrow the cause?
opts: The anion gap types a metabolic acidosis; it does not sort the causes of an alkalosis. Saline-unresponsive causes split by blood pressure. Tell: the gap belongs to acidosis.

Correct. A high urine chloride (above 40 mEq/L) means saline-unresponsive alkalosis, whose causes split by blood pressure: normotensive (severe potassium depletion, hypoparathyroidism and hypercalcemia) or hypertensive (primary aldosteronism, mineralocorticoids, licorice).
His expected carbon dioxide by Winter
The Winter formula checks compensation in metabolic acidosis. His disorder is an alkalosis, and the cause list splits by blood pressure. Tell: Winter is for acidosis.
His urine chloride is already high, placing him in the saline-unresponsive group; repeating it adds nothing. The next split is by blood pressure. Tell: urine chloride first, then blood pressure.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
A.q: A 39-year-old man with asthma takes ibuprofen for a sprained ankle. Within 20 minutes he develops a runny nose, red irritated eyes, facial flushing and wheezing. Which diagnosis explains the reaction?
opts: Exercise-induced bronchospasm follows exertion, and a sprained ankle is not exercise. Tell: the reaction followed a non-selective anti-inflammatory drug and included flushing, rhinorrhea and eye irritation, the aspirin-sensitive picture.
ruled out by a stated finding

Cardiac asthma is wheezing from decompensated heart failure, and he has no heart failure. Tell: wheeze with flushing, a runny nose and eye irritation minutes after ibuprofen is a drug reaction, not a cardiac cause.
ruled out by a stated finding

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity to the Aspergillus mold, not to a drug. Tell: the timing after ibuprofen and the flushing and eye symptoms identify aspirin sensitivity with cross-reactivity to a non-selective agent.

Correct. About 1 to 5% of asthmatics worsen with aspirin, and patients with true aspirin sensitivity cross-react with non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen. Rhinorrhea, conjunctival irritation, facial flushing and wheezing within minutes of the dose is the described reaction.

A.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
A.q: A 39-year-old man with asthma took aspirin at noon for a headache and developed facial flushing, a runny nose and wheezing at about 10 that night. He asks whether the aspirin could be responsible so many hours later. Which reply is accurate?
opts: No, aspirin sensitivity causes rash alone
Aspirin-sensitive asthma causes rhinorrhea, conjunctival irritation, facial flushing and wheezing, not a rash alone. Tell: his runny nose, flushing and wheeze match the listed reaction exactly.
Yes, reactions can be delayed up to 12 hours

Correct. In aspirin-sensitive asthma, symptoms may occur within minutes of aspirin ingestion or may be delayed up to 12 hours, and they include rhinorrhea, conjunctival irritation, facial flushing and wheezing. His reaction 10 hours after the dose fits.

Reactions can occur within minutes but may also be delayed up to 12 hours, so a 10-hour gap does not rule out aspirin. Tell: the window extends to 12 hours, and his flushing, rhinorrhea and wheeze are the typical features.
Yes, but just selective agents cause it

The cross-reacting drugs are the non-selective anti-inflammatory agents, while selective ones such as celecoxib may be used. Tell: aspirin itself caused this reaction, which can be delayed up to 12 hours.

A.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
A.q: A 69-year-old woman with chronic lung disease is assessed for home oxygen before discharge. Her resting room-air saturation is exactly 88%, and she has no other findings. What is her qualification?
opts: Group II is for a saturation of 89% (or arterial oxygen pressure of 56-59 mm Hg) plus pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or a hematocrit above 56%, recertified at 3 months. Her 88% already meets Group I. Tell: 88% or less is Group I; 89% needs a comorbidity.

Correct. Group I qualifies at a resting room-air saturation of 88% or less, and hers is exactly 88%, which meets the cutoff. Group I patients are recertified at 12 months, and no comorbidity is needed.

Exertion oxygen requires a saturation of 88% or less with activity that improves with oxygen. No exertion testing is described, and her resting value already qualifies her at rest. Tell: she qualifies at rest, which is a stronger finding.
A comorbidity is needed only when the saturation is 89%. At 88% she meets the Group I rest criterion as is. Tell: the boundary 88% counts; the comorbidity requirement begins at 89%.

A.q: A 40-year-old woman is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. She has never been tested for human immunodeficiency virus infection. Which additional test should be offered?
opts: A skin test detects the immune response to infection and cannot distinguish latent infection from disease, so it does not move her care forward. Tell: her unknown virus status is the gap the workup closes.

Imaging supports suspicion but cannot confirm tuberculosis or reliably determine activity, so weekly films do not guide care. Tell: the test the workup adds for her is human immunodeficiency virus testing.
The blood test detects the immune response to infection, not disease, and her diagnosis is already made. Tell: when virus status is unknown, the workup offers human immunodeficiency virus testing.

Correct. The microbiologic evaluation of suspected pulmonary tuberculosis includes offering human immunodeficiency virus testing when status is unknown. Infection with the virus is one of the higher progression risks and can produce atypical radiographic patterns.

A.q: A 62-year-old man's chest radiograph and sputum smear lead his clinician to presume pulmonary tuberculosis; culture results are weeks away. Which reporting step is appropriate now?
opts: Reporting covers presumed as well as confirmed tuberculosis, and cultures can take weeks. Tell: a presumed case is reported to the local or state tuberculosis program now.
No report; the clinician manages it
Tuberculosis care is coordinated with the local or state tuberculosis program, and isolation ends by public-health criteria among others. Tell: a presumed case is reported now, not managed privately.
Report if drug resistance is found

Notification is for every presumed or confirmed case, not just resistant ones; rifampin resistance additionally needs rapid susceptibility testing and expert management. Tell: resistance changes the regimen, not whether to report.

Correct. The local or state tuberculosis program is notified of presumed or confirmed tuberculosis, so reporting does not wait for culture. Public-health coordination also guides the criteria for ending isolation.

A.q: A 57-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has 4 weeks of fevers, sweats, fatigue and a cough with foul-smelling purulent sputum. A chest radiograph shows a cavity with an air-fluid level. Which initial therapy is most appropriate?
opts: Clindamycin is reserved for selected alternatives because of Clostridioides difficile risk. Tell: the usual first choice for lung abscess is a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor such as ampicillin-sulbactam.

Correct. A cavity with an air-fluid level after weeks of fever and foul sputum is a lung abscess, which usually begins with antibiotics. A beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor is the usual first choice, such as intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam followed by oral amoxicillin-clavulanate, often for several weeks.

Routine chest physiotherapy is not essential in lung abscess. Tell: the treatment is antibiotics for several weeks, guided by clinical and radiographic response, with drainage only for large or refractory abscesses.

Drainage or surgery is for large or refractory abscesses after pulmonary or infectious disease review, while lung abscess usually begins with antibiotics. Tell: surgery is the escalation, not the starting point.

A.q: A 71-year-old man treated for right lower lobe community-acquired pneumonia is worse on day 4 of appropriate antibiotics. His chest radiograph now shows a patchy, nonhomogeneous opacity, and atelectasis hides the lower lobes. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Antibiotics are not withheld when bacterial pneumonia is suspected or the course worsens; the response to failure is reassessment, not withdrawal. Tell: a worsening bacterial pneumonia needs its cause found while treatment continues.

Correct. Worsening on therapy calls for reassessing the diagnosis and looking for an abscess, empyema or another complication. Computed tomography follows the radiograph when the opacity is not homogeneous or atelectasis prevents seeing the lower lobes, and it finds the complication or alternative cause that changes drainage or treatment.

When the course worsens, reassess the diagnosis, resistance risk, adherence and complications instead of reflexively adding drugs. He needs the cause of failure found first. Tell: imaging comes before escalation when a film cannot show the lower lobes.

A delayed film leaves a worsening patient unexplained, and his radiograph already cannot show the lower lobes, one of the stated reasons for computed tomography now. Tell: worsening on therapy is a problem for today, not for a follow-up film.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
A.q: An 84-year-old woman has mild breathlessness she attributes to deconditioning. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows a ratio of 0.68 with a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 85% predicted. Which consideration applies before labeling her with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: Correct. In adults 65 and older, the fixed 0.70 ratio may overdiagnose, so clinical context is weighed. A borderline ratio with near-normal airflow and mild symptoms in an 84-year-old calls for that judgment.
Triple therapy is considered for high-risk group E patients with eosinophils of 300 or more. Tell: she has not even been confirmed, and her symptoms are mild.
In older adults the fixed 0.70 ratio may overdiagnose. Tell: her age and borderline value call for clinical context, not an automatic label.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin testing is aimed at young patients or those with few exposures, and mild breathlessness at 84 with a borderline ratio does not point to it. Tell: in an elderly patient the stated caution is overdiagnosis from the fixed ratio.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
A.q: Frequent use of a short-acting bronchodilator signals which problem in asthma?
opts: Taking the short-acting agent before exercise is the right use in exercise-induced bronchospasm and is planned, not frequent symptom relief. Frequent use for symptoms signals poorly controlled asthma. Tell: pre-exercise dosing is prevention; repeated use for symptoms is a control problem.
Expected tolerance that needs no change
Frequent rescue use is not a benign tolerance effect to accept. It signals poor control and calls for reviewing the controller and compliance.
Well controlled disease using rescue as intended
Frequent rescue use is the warning sign of poor control, not evidence of good control, and it is listed among the risks of death.
Poorly controlled disease with higher risk of death

Correct. Frequent bronchodilator use marks poorly controlled asthma, one of the listed risks of death, and increased rescue use usually signifies poor control. It should prompt a review of controller therapy, compliance and inhaler technique.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. A.q: A 32-year-old man who received BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) vaccine in infancy needs testing for tuberculosis infection before starting work in a setting with ongoing transmission. He has no symptoms. Which test is preferred?
opts: Sputum testing is for suspected pulmonary disease, driven by symptoms or suspicious imaging, and a smear cannot separate tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria. Tell: he is symptom-free, so the question is infection, answered by an immune-response test.

The skin test can be falsely positive after bacille Calmette-Guérin vaccination or some nontuberculous exposures. Tell: for a vaccinated patient the interferon-gamma release assay is preferred, since vaccination does not make it positive.

Correct. Bacille Calmette-Guérin vaccination can cause a false-positive skin test, and the blood test is preferred for most vaccinated patients because the vaccine does not cause a positive interferon-gamma release assay. It measures immune responses to tuberculosis-specific antigens and needs one visit.

Computed tomography can clarify radiograph findings or complications, but imaging cannot confirm tuberculosis or detect infection. Tell: screening for infection uses an immune-response test, and the blood test suits a vaccinated man.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for mycobacterial infections for the following populations. 3. adult 4. elderly
A.q: Which age group is named as a higher-progression-risk group after tuberculosis infection?
opts: Early and middle adulthood are not listed as a progression risk group; infancy and young childhood are. Tell: risk is named at the start of life, not in the adult years.

Correct. Infancy and young childhood are listed with the higher progression risks, alongside human immunodeficiency virus infection or major immunosuppression, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, transplantation, prolonged corticosteroids and recent infection within 2 years.
Adolescence is not singled out as a progression risk; the age group listed is infancy and young childhood. Tell: the youngest children carry the higher risk.

Older adults are noted to present atypically with pulmonary tuberculosis, but the age group on the progression list is infancy and young childhood. Tell: atypical presentation and progression risk are different points.

A.q: A 35-year-old woman has had fever, sore throat and cough since yesterday. A single home antigen test for coronavirus disease 2019 is negative. What is the most appropriate next step in testing?
opts: A D-dimer level to confirm it

D-dimer elevation does not diagnose thrombosis, let alone viral infection, and hospital tests should answer a specific clinical question. Tell: diagnosing coronavirus infection takes a repeat antigen test or a nucleic acid test.
Chest imaging to find the virus

Chest imaging evaluates pneumonia and complications, not the viral cause. She has no sign of pneumonia, and imaging cannot confirm the coronavirus. Tell: identifying the virus takes a repeat antigen test or a nucleic acid test.
Repeat the antigen test after 48 hours

Correct. One negative antigen test does not exclude infection. A symptomatic person repeats the test after 48 hours for at least 2 tests, or obtains a nucleic acid amplification test, the most sensitive routine method. Her symptoms make the single negative result unreliable.

A single negative antigen test does not exclude coronavirus infection. Tell: a symptomatic person needs at least 2 antigen tests, 48 hours apart, or a nucleic acid amplification test before infection is called negative.

A.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
A.q: A 52-year-old man has hypertension that is hard to control and muscle weakness. He takes no diuretics, has not vomited, and eats a bag of black licorice every day. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.47 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 47 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 33 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); potassium 3.0 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L); urine chloride is high. Which part of his history best accounts for this blood gas?
opts: Correct. High pH with a high bicarbonate is metabolic alkalosis; the high urine chloride makes it saline unresponsive, and his high blood pressure puts it in the hypertensive group, which lists licorice. Low potassium with weakness fits.

Vomiting (loss of hydrochloric acid) causes a saline-responsive alkalosis with a low urine chloride, below 25 mEq/L, and volume contraction. His urine chloride is high and he is hypertensive. Tell: vomiting-type alkalosis has a low urine chloride.
ruled out by a stated finding

Hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis, with a carbon dioxide below 36. His is 47 and his bicarbonate 33, so the primary change is metabolic. Tell: respiratory alkalosis lowers the carbon dioxide; his is raised as compensation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Antacids cause a saline-responsive alkalosis, with a low urine chloride. His is high, and he is hypertensive rather than volume contracted. Tell: a high urine chloride steers you to the saline-unresponsive list.
ruled out by a stated finding
