B.q: A 77-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia has a PSI (Pneumonia Severity Index) total of 104 points. Which risk class does that total fall in?
opts: Class II covers 51 to 70 points, with a mortality of 0.6%. His 104 points are far above it. Tell: Class II is the low end of the scored classes, and a total over 100 cannot sit there.
Class III covers 71 to 90 points, with a mortality of 0.9%. His 104 points are above that band. Tell: once a total passes 90 it moves to Class IV, where mortality jumps about tenfold, to 9.3%.

Correct. On the interpretation table, 91 to 130 points is Class IV, with a mortality of 9.3%. The index plus clinical judgment is the preferred support for the admission decision, and a total just over 100 already carries roughly a 1 in 10 risk of death.
Class V starts at 131 points, with a mortality of 27.0%. His 104 points fall short of it. Tell: Class IV runs from 91 to 130, so 104 is a Class IV total.

B.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
B.q: A 67-year-old man has a post-bronchodilator ratio of 0.55 and a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 34% predicted. Which airflow grade fits?
opts: Grade 1, mild, needs 80% predicted or more; at 34% he is far below. Tell: grade 1 is near-normal airflow, and he has about a third of predicted. His ratio confirms obstruction; the grade then depends on the 1-second volume.
Grade 2, moderate, covers 50% up to 80% predicted; 34% is below that range. Tell: under 50% the grade is at least severe. Moderate means at least half of predicted airflow, which he does not have.
Correct. With the ratio below 0.70, the grade comes from the post-bronchodilator 1-second volume: 34% sits in the 30% to 49% band, grade 3, severe. Grade 4 would need less than 30%.
Grade 4, very severe, is below 30% predicted. At 34% he is just above that cutoff. Tell: 30% to 49% is grade 3, so 34% stays severe. A 4-point margin still counts; the bands do not round.

B.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
B.q: A 24-year-old woman started an inhaled corticosteroid for moderate persistent asthma 1 week ago and wants to stop it because she does not feel much different yet. What should she be told?
opts: Relief within minutes describes a short-acting beta-2 agonist, which relaxes smooth muscle and lasts about 3 to 6 hours. Tell: inhaled corticosteroids reduce inflammation slowly, with maximum response taking months.
Her lack of change means she needs oral steroids
Long-term systemic steroids are for refractory or poorly controlled cases, and 1 week cannot show failure of an inhaled steroid. Tell: maximum response to inhaled corticosteroids may take months.
It is meant to be used during attacks

Inhaled corticosteroids are long-term controllers, not rescue medicines; attacks are treated with the short-acting rescue inhaler. Tell: a controller is taken every day and works gradually, over months.
Its full effect can take months

Correct. Inhaled corticosteroids are the preferred first-line treatment for persistent asthma, and most patients respond to twice-daily dosing, but the maximum response may take months. One week is too early to judge, and stopping would leave her inflammation untreated.

B.io: Identify and discuss vaccines which prevent respiratory infections.
B.q: A 26-year-old woman who is 14 weeks pregnant comes in during October and asks about vaccines. Which vaccine should be avoided during her pregnancy?
opts: An age-appropriate recombinant vaccine may be used in any trimester of pregnancy. Tell: inactivated and recombinant vaccines are both acceptable; the live attenuated vaccine is the one avoided.
An age-appropriate inactivated vaccine is recommended in any trimester of pregnancy. Tell: the restriction in pregnancy is on the live attenuated product, not on inactivated vaccine.
Tdap is given during every pregnancy to protect against pertussis. Tell: Tdap is one of the vaccines recommended in pregnancy, so it is not the one to avoid.

Correct. In pregnancy, influenza vaccination uses an age-appropriate inactivated or recombinant vaccine in any trimester, and the live attenuated vaccine is avoided. Live attenuated vaccine has pregnancy and immunocompromise restrictions, so her pregnancy rules it out.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: A 36-year-old man with advanced human immunodeficiency virus infection has 4 weeks of cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss. His interferon-gamma release assay is negative. Which next step is most appropriate?
opts: Latent-infection treatment requires disease to be excluded first. Tell: cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss in an immunosuppressed man are possible disease, the opposite of a cleared evaluation.
Repeat the assay in 8 to 10 weeks
Repeat testing 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure is for a symptom-free recent contact with an early negative result. Tell: he has symptoms of disease now, which require evaluation now.
Accept the negative assay as reassuring
A negative assay makes infection less likely, but disease remains possible, and immunosuppression reduces sensitivity. Tell: his symptoms demand microbiologic testing regardless of the blood test.

Correct. Symptoms or high clinical suspicion require evaluation for disease now, with microbiologic testing even when the skin test or assay is negative. Immunosuppression reduces assay sensitivity and can cause false negatives, so sputum specimens go for smear, culture and a rapid molecular test.

B.q: An 80-year-old woman from a nursing home is admitted with fever, cough and shortness of breath while both influenza and coronavirus disease 2019 are circulating in the community. Which test should be sent?
opts: Cultures are obtained for severe community-acquired pneumonia or validated resistant-pathogen risk, and a bacterial culture detects neither virus. Tell: the co-circulation clue asks which virus she has, which a molecular test answers.

Correct. Hospitalized patients are tested with a molecular assay, and a multiplex influenza and coronavirus test is useful during co-circulation. Her age, nursing-home residence and admission make the result important for antivirals and infection prevention.

Rapid antigen tests have limited sensitivity and do not test for the coronavirus. Hospitalized patients are tested with a molecular assay. Tell: with both viruses circulating, one molecular multiplex test answers both questions.

Viral culture is mainly for surveillance and does not guide time-sensitive treatment. Tell: an admitted patient needs a fast molecular result that can change antiviral treatment and precautions today.

B.q: A 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and chronic heart failure has community-acquired pneumonia and is stable for outpatient care. Molecular testing is positive for a respiratory virus, and she asks to skip antibiotics because a friend with the same result did. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Viral-positive patients with comorbidities generally still need empiric antibacterial therapy. Diabetes and chronic heart disease are listed comorbidities, so the outpatient regimen is amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefpodoxime or cefuroxime plus azithromycin or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone.

Avoiding empiric antibiotics with close follow-up is reserved for viral-positive outpatients without comorbidities. She has diabetes and heart failure. Tell: the viral result helps only a patient without comorbidities; hers keep the antibiotic.
ruled out by a stated finding

Doxycycline by itself is an outpatient option for a patient without comorbidities. With her diabetes and heart failure, doxycycline is a partner to a beta-lactam such as cefpodoxime, not a solo drug. Tell: comorbidities turn monotherapy into a combination.

Amoxicillin by itself is the outpatient choice for patients with no comorbidities and no resistant-organism risk. Her diabetes and heart failure call for a beta-lactam combination or a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Tell: comorbidities upgrade the regimen.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 33-year-old man with human immunodeficiency virus infection has never had Pneumocystis pneumonia. His CD4 (cluster of differentiation 4) count is 160 cells/mm³, and his viral load is detectable. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: No prophylaxis while he feels well

Prophylaxis is decided by the count and the viral load, not by symptoms; waiting for symptoms means waiting for the infection. Tell: a count of 160 with a detectable viral load qualifies him whether or not he feels well.

Secondary prophylaxis follows a completed treatment course, but primary prophylaxis is meant to prevent the first episode in patients who meet the count criteria. Tell: he has never had the infection and already qualifies for primary prophylaxis.

Correct. Primary prophylaxis starts for a CD4 (cluster of differentiation 4) count below 100 cells/mm³, or a count of 100 to 200 with a detectable viral load. His 160 with a detectable viral load meets the second criterion, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the preferred drug.
Wait until the count is below 100

Below 100 is one trigger, but a count of 100 to 200 with a detectable viral load is the other, and he meets it. Tell: read both parts of the criterion; his detectable viral load brings the threshold up to 200.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. B.q: A 63-year-old woman hospitalized with coronavirus disease 2019 and hypoxemia is on dexamethasone, but over 24 hours she needs rapidly increasing oxygen. Which treatment should be added?
opts: Molnupiravir is an early outpatient alternative when preferred options are unsuitable, not a hospital escalation for hypoxemia. Tell: the escalation drugs for rapid progression are baricitinib or tocilizumab.

Antibacterial treatment is not used for coronavirus disease 2019 without a bacterial complication, and none is described. Tell: her worsening is viral and inflammatory progression, which baricitinib or tocilizumab addresses.
Baricitinib or tocilizumab is added to corticosteroids, not used in their place. Tell: rapid progression escalates therapy on top of dexamethasone; stopping the steroid removes the core treatment.

Correct. Rapid progression in a hospitalized patient may warrant baricitinib or tocilizumab in addition to corticosteroids, along with appropriate oxygen or ventilatory support. Her rising oxygen needs on dexamethasone are that rapid progression.

B.io: Identify compensatory mechanisms for simple acid-base disorders.
B.q: A 21-year-old woman in diabetic ketoacidosis has Kussmaul respirations (deep, rapid breathing). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.22 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 20 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 8 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What does her breathing pattern accomplish?
opts: It lowers carbon dioxide to offset the acidosis

Correct. Metabolic acidosis is compensated by increased ventilation to decrease carbon dioxide; in severe cases hyperventilation is profound, as Kussmaul respirations (increased tidal volume and tachypnea) in diabetic ketoacidosis. Her carbon dioxide of 20 shows it.
It is a primary respiratory alkalosis

A primary respiratory alkalosis would raise the pH above 7.45. Hers is 7.22, so her low carbon dioxide is compensation for the metabolic acidosis. Tell: low carbon dioxide with a low pH is compensation.

Impending respiratory failure is suggested when carbon dioxide is higher than the Winter formula predicts (1.5 x 8 + 8 = 20, plus or minus 2). Hers is 20, right on target. Tell: a tiring patient's carbon dioxide drifts up, not down.
It retains carbon dioxide to raise her pH
Retaining carbon dioxide would lower the pH; it is how the lungs compensate a metabolic alkalosis. Deep, rapid breathing removes carbon dioxide. Tell: fast, deep breathing lowers carbon dioxide.
B.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 50

B.io: Identify mechanisms for maintaining acid-base homeostasis.
B.q: A 38-year-old woman develops an acute respiratory acidosis after aspiration pneumonitis two hours ago. When will her kidneys begin to compensate?
opts: In 6 to 12 hours, completing over days

Correct. In respiratory acidosis the kidneys excrete acid as ammonium chloride and retain bicarbonate; this begins 6 to 12 hours after onset, and complete compensation may take days. At two hours her bicarbonate is near normal.
Within minutes, completing in an hour
Breathing changes carbon dioxide quickly, but renal bicarbonate control works over hours to days. Tell: the kidneys are the slow system.
They do not; the lungs compensate instead
When the cause is respiratory, the compensation is renal: the kidneys retain or excrete bicarbonate. The lungs compensate for metabolic disorders. Tell: respiratory problem, renal fix.
Renal compensation begins within 6 to 12 hours and may be complete in days, not weeks. Tell: hours to start, days to finish.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: A 43-year-old woman with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis has three sputum specimens collected. Which testing should be requested on the specimens?
opts: Molecular test in place of culture

A rapid molecular test is performed on at least one specimen, but alongside, not instead of, mycobacterial culture; culture also supplies culture-based susceptibility testing. Tell: smear and culture stay in the request.
Gram stain and routine bacterial culture

Acid-fast organisms are looked for with an acid-fast smear and a mycobacterial culture, not routine bacterial testing. Tell: the request names the smear, the mycobacterial culture and a rapid molecular test.
Acid-fast smear, culture and a molecular test

Correct. The specimens go for acid-fast smear and mycobacterial culture, a rapid molecular test is performed on at least one respiratory specimen, and molecular and culture-based drug-susceptibility testing is obtained.
Acid-fast smear, then stop if negative

A smear is one part of the workup, and slow-growing cultures can take weeks to answer what a negative smear cannot. Tell: smear, culture and a rapid molecular test are requested together from the start.

B.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
B.q: A 67-year-old man on home oxygen for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease arrives with burns to his lips and nose after lighting a cigarette while wearing his cannula. Which hazard does this show?
opts: Correct. A man on home oxygen lights a cigarette while wearing his cannula and burns his lips and nose. Oxygen is highly flammable, and fire is a listed hazard of oxygen therapy, which is why no smoking is taught for every home oxygen user.

Mucosal irritation is dryness or soreness of the nasal lining from oxygen, usually at higher flows without humidity. It does not involve burns from an ignition source. Tell: dry, irritated mucosa is mucosal irritation; burns after a lit cigarette are fire.

Vasoconstriction is the effect of oxygen in a myocardial infarction, not a burn mechanism. His injury came from an open flame. Tell: a burn from an ignition source is fire; vasoconstriction is a cardiac concern when oxygen is not needed.

Hypercapnia, or carbon dioxide retention, is a listed hazard of oxygen, but it is retained gas, not a burn. His injury is burns after a lit cigarette. Tell: burns from a flame mean fire, not carbon dioxide.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for respiratory infections in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
B.q: A 68-year-old man with diabetes has mild coronavirus disease 2019 that began 2 days ago. His oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. He asks for the steroid his brother received in the hospital. Which treatment should be avoided?
opts: Supportive care is part of every coronavirus pathway and carries no special risk for him. Tell: the treatment to avoid is the one with a stated restriction, a steroid without hypoxemia.

Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir within 5 days is a preferred option for a high-risk outpatient with mild disease, and his age and diabetes make him high risk. Tell: review his drug interactions and kidney and liver issues, then treat; this is an indicated drug.

A three-day intravenous remdesivir course within 7 days of onset is a preferred early option for a high-risk outpatient like him. Tell: it is one of the two preferred antivirals, not something to avoid.

Correct. Systemic corticosteroids are not used for coronavirus disease 2019 without hypoxemia unless another indication exists. His saturation is 97% on room air, so a steroid adds risk, including to his blood glucose, without benefit; his brother's dexamethasone belonged to the hospital pathway for hypoxemia.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 78-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has an exacerbation. After treatment in the office his breathing is somewhat better, but he has new swelling of both legs, he lives alone, and he has no one to help at home. Which step is most appropriate?
opts: Rehabilitation is considered at discharge after an exacerbation, not as acute treatment. Tell: his new edema and lack of support at home call for admission first.

More than 80% of exacerbations can be managed outpatient, but his new edema and lack of home resources are listed admission criteria. Tell: who can care for the patient at home is part of the decision.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Admission criteria include new physical signs such as edema, significant comorbidities with an exacerbation, age, and lack of home or outpatient resources. His new edema, advanced age and lack of support at home meet several of them.

Intensive care is for hemodynamic instability, major infection, need for invasive ventilation, sepsis, altered mental status or respiratory acidosis. Nothing in his history suggests these. Tell: a ward admission fits his criteria.

B.topic: Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap
B.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
B.q: What is the treatment of metabolic acidosis, whether the anion gap is normal or elevated?
opts: Stopping diuretics is part of treating saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis. Metabolic acidosis is treated by treating its underlying disorder. Tell: diuretics are a cause of the alkalosis.
Give isotonic saline for every case

Isotonic saline treats saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, and saline infusion is itself a cause of normal-gap acidosis. The treatment is to treat the underlying disorder. Tell: saline fits the alkalosis, not the acidosis.
Correct. For both increased and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, the treatment is to treat the underlying disorder. The compensatory response is also assessed, using the Winter formula.

A paper bag is not necessary even in hyperventilation, where it fails to correct carbon dioxide and has only a placebo effect. Metabolic acidosis is treated by treating the underlying disorder. Tell: the gap type does not change the treatment, which targets the cause.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 67-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has 5 days of worsening breathlessness, and his usual white sputum has become larger in volume and yellow-green. He is alert with stable vital signs and has no history of resistant organisms or Pseudomonas. Which oral antibiotic is most appropriate?
opts: Levofloxacin is chosen for pseudomonal concern, and respiratory fluoroquinolones are used when resistance is a problem. He has neither. Tell: an uncomplicated exacerbation starts with doxycycline or a similar first-line agent.

Correct. Antibiotics are given when shortness of breath comes with increased sputum volume and purulence over baseline, as here. For an uncomplicated exacerbation, doxycycline, a macrolide, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or amoxicillin-clavulanate is considered.

Intravenous antibiotics are guided by systemic or severe infection affecting oxygen saturation and vital signs, raised lactate or white count, or need for ventilatory support. He is alert and stable. Tell: an oral first-line agent fits.
Antibiotics are indicated when breathlessness comes with more sputum that is also more purulent, and he has both changes. Tell: the sputum change is the trigger for treatment.

B.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
B.q: A 23-year-old woman has a panic attack before an exam, with light-headedness, perioral numbness and paresthesias (tingling) in both hands. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.53 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 27 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 22 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: Respiratory acidosis is a low pH with a high carbon dioxide. Her pH is 7.53 with a carbon dioxide of 27, the reverse. Tell: an alkalemic pH with a low carbon dioxide cannot be a primary respiratory acidosis, which needs a high carbon dioxide.

Metabolic alkalosis needs a high bicarbonate, and hers is 22, at the low edge of normal. The low carbon dioxide of 27 is what matches her alkalemia. Tell: in a respiratory alkalosis the bicarbonate is normal or low.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. The pH of 7.53 is alkalemia, and the carbon dioxide of 27 is low and matches it, so it is respiratory. Acutely, bicarbonate falls about 2 per 10 mm Hg fall in carbon dioxide: 13 below 40 predicts about 2.6 below the midpoint of 24, roughly 21 to 22, which matches her 22. Psychogenic hyperventilation is a listed cause, and perioral numbness is a listed finding.

Chronic respiratory alkalosis would lower bicarbonate about 5 per 10 mm Hg, to about 18 here (13 mm Hg below 40). Her 22 is the small acute fall. Tell: a bicarbonate of 22 fits the small acute fall; a chronic fall would take it near 18.

B.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
B.q: A 71-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure from lung disease) has an arterial oxygen pressure of 58 mm Hg at rest. What is his qualification status?
opts: Group I requires an arterial oxygen pressure of 55 mm Hg or less (or a saturation of 88% or less) at rest and is recertified at 12 months. His 58 mm Hg is above that, so he qualifies only through his comorbidity. Tell: 55 or less is Group I; 56-59 plus a comorbidity is Group II.

His data are resting values, and sleep qualification needs a saturation of 88% or less with a drop of 5% or more from baseline. Nothing about sleep is described. Tell: this is a resting qualification with a comorbidity.

Correct. His arterial oxygen pressure of 58 mm Hg is above the Group I limit of 55 mm Hg but within the 56-59 range, which qualifies only with a comorbidity. He has cor pulmonale, so he is Group II, and Group II is recertified at 3 months.

He does qualify: 58 mm Hg falls in the 56-59 range, and cor pulmonale is a qualifying comorbidity. The pressure alone would fall short, but together they meet Group II. Tell: the middle range qualifies once a listed comorbidity is present.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
B.q: On a Venturi mask, what changes the fraction of inspired oxygen delivered?
opts: Opening a one-way valve is not how a Venturi mask changes its fraction; the one-way valve belongs to the non-rebreather mask, where it prevents inhaling exhaled air. On a Venturi mask, different ports change the fraction. Tell: ports set the Venturi fraction.
Correct. On a Venturi mask, different ports change the fraction of inspired oxygen delivered, and the flow can be adjusted from 4 to 10 L/min to create 24% to 50%. The port is the control.

Tightening the head strap does not change the fraction delivered by a Venturi mask. Different ports change the fraction of inspired oxygen. Tell: the Venturi control is the port, which sets the precise fraction.

Inflating a reservoir bag is not how a Venturi mask sets its fraction; it has ports that change the amount delivered. Reservoir bags belong to the partial and non-rebreather masks. Tell: the Venturi mask changes by port.

B.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
B.q: A 73-year-old man with confirmed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a symptom assessment test score of 24 and a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 3. He had 3 moderate exacerbations in the past year. Using the 2020 four-group scheme, which group is he in?
opts: Group B has more symptoms but low risk. With 3 exacerbations he is high risk. Tell: high risk moves a symptomatic patient from B to D. B would fit only if he had 0 or 1 exacerbation without admission.
Group C is high risk with few symptoms; his score of 24 and grade 3 are heavy symptoms. Tell: high risk plus more symptoms is D. Both of his symptom measures are above the line.
Group E is the current three-group label for any high-risk patient. Tell: the question asks for the 2020 scheme, where he is D. In the 2020 scheme, the high-risk row splits into C and D by symptoms.

Correct. A symptom score of 24 and a dyspnea grade of 3 mean more symptoms, and 3 moderate exacerbations mean high risk. In the 2020 scheme, more symptoms with high risk is group D (group E in the current scheme).

B.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
B.q: A 71-year-old man starting home oxygen asks why he must be so careful at home if oxygen is "just air." Which property of oxygen underlies the safety teaching?
opts: Correct. Oxygen is highly flammable, which is why home oxygen teaching includes no smoking in the home, staying away from heat sources, avoiding petroleum products and posting signs. Oxygen is not just air, and fire is a listed hazard.
Oxygen being heavier than water is not a property stated and has no bearing on the teaching. The reason for the care is that oxygen is highly flammable. Tell: the key property is flammability.
It is toxic to breathe for visitors
Oxygen is not described as toxic to visitors. The hazards listed are carbon dioxide retention, fire, mucosal irritation and vasoconstriction. Tell: the home safety teaching rests on flammability.

Oxygen does not turn into carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide appears in the teaching only as a reason for working carbon monoxide alarms. Tell: alarms detect carbon monoxide; flammability is the property of oxygen.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 67-year-old woman with community-acquired pneumonia is newly disoriented to time and place. Her blood urea nitrogen is 19 mg/dL, respiratory rate 26/min and blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg. What is her CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or older) score?
opts: A total of 1 misses one of her two points. New disorientation to time and place is the confusion item, and age 67 is the age item. Tell: confusion means new disorientation to person, place or time, which she has.

Correct. Confusion 1 (new disorientation to time and place) + urea 0 (19 is not above 20) + respiratory rate 0 (26 is below 30) + blood pressure 0 (systolic 104, diastolic 66) + age 1 (67) = 2. That is moderate severity, with a risk of death of 9%, and the pathway places her in the hospital.

A total of 3 adds urea or respiratory rate, but neither meets its threshold: urea 19 mg/dL is not above 20, and a respiratory rate of 26 is below 30. Tell: both sit under their cut-offs, so neither scores, and she stays at 2.

A total of 4 would need two of urea, respiratory rate and blood pressure, and none of them qualifies: urea 19 (needs above 20), respiratory rate 26 (needs 30), systolic 104 and diastolic 66. Tell: only confusion and age count.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 63-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a daytime resting oxygen saturation of 94% and normal saturation while walking, but overnight oximetry shows saturations of 86% at night only. Which step is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Desaturation to 88% or less at night only calls for evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea and screening for other causes, rather than long-term oxygen. His daytime resting and exertional saturations are normal.
Nighttime desaturation is not ignored; it prompts evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea and other causes. Tell: night-only desaturation has its own branch of the oxygen pathway.
Exertional oxygen is for desaturation to 88% or less with exercise, and his saturation stays normal while walking. Tell: his only drop is overnight, which points to a sleep evaluation.
ruled out by a stated finding
Long-term oxygen over 15 hours a day
Long-term oxygen for more than 15 hours a day is for severe resting desaturation while awake, 88% or less. His daytime resting value is 94%. Tell: night-only drops lead to a sleep evaluation first.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
B.q: Which physical findings may accompany extrinsic (allergic) asthma?
opts: Cyanosis, edema, and distended neck veins

Cyanosis, edema and distended neck veins describe right heart strain in chronic lung disease, not the allergic findings of extrinsic asthma. Tell: allergic asthma shows its atopy in the nose and skin, not in signs of heart failure.
Swollen nasal mucosa, eczema, and nasal polyps

Correct. Extrinsic, allergic asthma may bring swelling of the nasal mucosa, increased secretions, atopic dermatitis or eczema, and nasal polyps, even when the chest exam is clear between attacks. These reflect the atopic triad of rhinitis, asthma and dermatitis.

These suggest chronic infection, fibrosis or malignancy, not allergy. Extrinsic asthma may show nasal mucosal swelling, increased secretions, eczema and nasal polyps. Tell: the allergic findings match the atopic triad, nose and skin.

These belong to a systemic autoimmune disease, not to allergic asthma. The allergic asthma findings are nasal swelling and secretions, eczema and nasal polyps. Tell: atopic skin disease is eczema, not a facial butterfly rash.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
B.q: A 19-year-old college student has had episodes of wheezing, chest tightness and cough for 2 years, worse at night and after cleaning his dusty dorm room. He has allergic rhinitis and atopic dermatitis (eczema). Between episodes his lung exam is normal. Spirometry shows a reduced forced expiratory volume in 1 second that improves 18% after albuterol. Which diagnosis is most likely?
opts: Intrinsic asthma is non-atopic and of later, adult onset, often with nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity. This 19-year-old has rhinitis, eczema and a dust trigger, an atopic picture. Tell: the atopic triad and an allergen trigger point to extrinsic, not intrinsic, asthma.
ruled out by a stated finding

Vocal fold dysfunction is an upper airway mimic in the differential, but it would not produce reversible lower airway obstruction on spirometry or travel with eczema and rhinitis. Tell: reversible obstruction plus atopy places the problem in the lower airways, not the larynx.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a lower airway mimic, but its obstruction is largely irreversible and it follows years of smoke exposure. This student's obstruction reversed by 18% after albuterol. Tell: a large bronchodilator response in a young atopic patient supports asthma.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Episodic wheeze, chest tightness and cough worse at night, a dust trigger, allergic rhinitis and eczema (the atopic triad), a normal exam between episodes, and an 18% rise in the 1-second volume after albuterol (12% or more is a positive response) make allergic, extrinsic asthma the diagnosis.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
B.q: How is exercise-induced bronchospasm best prevented?
opts: A long-acting beta-2 agonist must not be used as monotherapy because it has no anti-inflammatory effect. Regular inhaled corticosteroids are the best prevention. Tell: any long-acting agent in asthma must ride with an inhaled corticosteroid.
ruled out by a stated finding
A goal of asthma care is no limitation on activity; medication, not avoidance, prevents the bronchospasm. Tell: the treatment plan protects participation in sport rather than removing it.

Theophylline is rarely used because of toxicity and is not the exercise strategy. Regular inhaled corticosteroids best prevent exercise-induced bronchospasm, with a short-acting inhaler before exercise. Tell: the pre-exercise drug is inhaled, not an oral methylxanthine.

Correct. Exercise-induced bronchospasm is treated with an inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist before exercise and is best prevented with regular inhaled corticosteroid use. It is common in children and adolescents, so this keeps teenagers in sport.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 66-year-old thin man with a long smoking history breathes through pursed lips. He has a barrel chest, distant breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion. His diffusing capacity is reduced, and he produces little sputum. Which subtype best describes his disease?
opts: Correct. A thin patient with pursed-lip breathing, barrel chest, distant breath sounds and hyperresonance, little sputum, and a reduced diffusing capacity is the classic emphysema picture (the pink puffer), from alveolar destruction and loss of elastic recoil.

Asthma's exam is often normal between exacerbations, and it does not destroy alveoli or lower diffusing capacity. Tell: a barrel chest with a reduced diffusing capacity in a long-time smoker is emphysema.

The chronic bronchitis subtype brings cough with sputum, rhonchi, possible cyanosis and edema, and a normal or near-normal diffusing capacity. He has little sputum and a reduced diffusing capacity. Tell: the reduced diffusing capacity singles out emphysema.
ruled out by a stated finding
Fibrosis is restrictive and shrinks the lungs, so hyperresonance and a barrel chest from hyperinflation do not fit. Tell: his findings show too much air in the chest, not too little.

B.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
B.q: A 24-year-old man with a panic attack is breathing fast, with perioral numbness and tingling hands. His roommate hands him a paper bag to breathe into. What is accurate education about the bag?
opts: It is unnecessary and may lower his oxygen

Correct. Breathing into a paper bag is not necessary for hyperventilation: it fails to correct the carbon dioxide and may decrease oxygen, and any benefit is placebo. Hyperventilation is usually self-limited, and the cause is treated.
It works by raising his bicarbonate
Rebreathing does not act on bicarbonate; bicarbonate changes come from the kidneys over hours to days. The bag's benefit is placebo. Tell: bicarbonate is renal and slow; no bag reaches it.
It safely corrects his carbon dioxide
The bag fails to correct carbon dioxide, and it may lower oxygen. Its effect is placebo. Tell: the paper bag fails on both counts, carbon dioxide and safety.
It is needed to prevent tetany

Tetany can occur in severe respiratory alkalosis from low ionized calcium, but the bag does not prevent it; hyperventilation is usually self-limited. Tell: treat the cause, not the carbon dioxide with a bag.

B.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
B.q: Which cause of respiratory alkalosis works through hypoxia-driven hyperventilation?
opts: Flail chest impairs ventilation and causes acute respiratory acidosis. High altitude drives hyperventilation through hypoxia. Tell: impaired ventilation raises carbon dioxide, hypoxic drive lowers it.

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome causes chronic respiratory acidosis through hypoventilation. High altitude causes hypoxia-driven respiratory alkalosis. Tell: hypoventilation raises carbon dioxide, hypoxic hyperventilation lowers it.

Correct. Hyperventilation secondary to hypoxia causes respiratory alkalosis, and high altitude is a listed example. The others on that list are severe anemia, ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypotension.

Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular cause of acute respiratory acidosis, from weakened breathing. High altitude drives hypoxic hyperventilation. Tell: hypoxia that increases breathing leads to alkalosis.

B.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
B.q: A 45-year-old woman with severe persistent asthma has needed 4 courses of oral corticosteroids this year despite confirmed adherence and good technique with her inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting beta-2 agonist. Which step is most appropriate?
opts: Refer to a lung or allergy specialist

Correct. With adherence and technique confirmed, her repeated steroid-requiring exacerbations make her asthma refractory. Monoclonal antibody agents are used by pulmonology and allergy specialists and reduced the need for corticosteroids in trials, so referral to a specialist fits.

Immunotherapy must be done in a controlled environment because it can induce bronchoconstriction, and it targets allergic triggers. Tell: her problem is refractory severe asthma, which calls for specialist care.

Removing part of a regimen she uses correctly would not explain or fix her exacerbations. Tell: refractory, steroid-dependent asthma despite adherence calls for a specialist, who can offer agents that reduce the need for steroids.

Theophylline gives mild bronchodilation but has a narrow toxic-therapeutic range and is rarely used because of toxicity concerns. Tell: refractory disease needing repeated steroids is a specialist referral, where steroid-sparing antibody therapy is available.

Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: Which presentation separates pneumonia from acute bronchitis?
opts: Correct. Apart from walking pneumonia, pneumonia presents more severely than bronchitis: higher fevers and chills, pleuritic or atypical chest pain, a productive cough and shortness of breath with tachypnea. Bronchitis tends to bring a low-grade fever.
Colored sputum occurs in both and does not separate viral from bacterial illness. Tell: severity (higher fever, tachypnea, focal findings) is what points to pneumonia.
A central, substernal wheeze over the bronchial airways is a feature of acute bronchitis. Tell: pneumonia shows focal findings such as crackles, dullness or consolidation, with tachypnea.
A low-grade fever with chills, body aches and fatigue is the cold-like start of acute bronchitis. Tell: pneumonia brings higher fevers and a faster breathing rate.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: Which statement about how often this disease is diagnosed is accurate?
opts: Most cases are diagnosed when symptoms begin
Many patients remain undiagnosed for years after symptoms start in midlife. Tell: the disease is underdiagnosed, partly because early symptoms are subtle.

Correct. Underdiagnosis is very common: many patients develop symptoms in midlife but remain undiagnosed until later adulthood. Symptoms may be subtle at first, such as exertional dyspnea, a prolonged expiratory phase or wheezing alone.
In older adults a fixed 0.70 ratio may overdiagnose, but overall underdiagnosis is very common. Tell: the general problem is missed disease in people with midlife symptoms.

Symptoms typically develop in midlife, not childhood; early onset raises suspicion of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Tell: the usual story is midlife symptoms with a diagnosis delayed until later adulthood.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 34-year-old woman has had a cough for 10 days that began with a cold. Her sputum is green, and she asks for an antibiotic. Her temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation are normal, and her lungs have scattered rhonchi that clear with coughing and no focal findings. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin are not default bronchitis treatments, and antibiotic harms include adverse effects, Clostridioides difficile infection and resistance. Tell: a respiratory fluoroquinolone belongs to the community-acquired pneumonia pathway, not to a viral chest cold with normal vital signs.

Correct. Normal vital signs, no focal lung findings and rhonchi that clear with a cough describe uncomplicated acute bronchitis, usually a self-limited viral illness. Green or yellow sputum does not separate viral from bacterial infection, so no antibiotic is given; explain the expected course and agree on symptom goals.

Amoxicillin-clavulanate is named as not a default bronchitis treatment, and routine antibiotics are not prescribed for uncomplicated bronchitis regardless of cough duration or sputum color. Her normal vital signs keep her out of the pneumonia pathway. Tell: green sputum alone never earns an antibiotic.

Routine sputum culture and chest radiography are unnecessary in uncomplicated cases; imaging is for abnormal vital signs, focal lung findings or clinical risk that raise concern for pneumonia. She has none of these. Tell: order a test only when its result would change a decision.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: A 50-year-old man is diagnosed with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis, and the health department is ranking his contacts. Which contact has the highest exposure risk?
opts: Cousin he visited once for an hour

A single 1-hour visit is brief compared with sharing an office, and risk rises with prolonged exposure in enclosed spaces. Tell: contacts are ranked by how long and how closely they shared air, and the office mate has far more of both.

Passing someone briefly is not prolonged exposure, and prolonged shared indoor air is what raises risk. Tell: rank contacts by how long and how closely they shared enclosed, poorly ventilated air with him.
Neighbor who chatted with him outdoors
Risk increases with prolonged shared indoor air and poor ventilation. Tell: a short conversation outdoors has neither feature, so it carries far less exposure than shared office air.
Office mate in a small unventilated room

Correct. Exposure risk rises with close contact with a person who has infectious tuberculosis and with prolonged exposure in enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces. Sharing a small unventilated office combines both, giving the most prolonged shared indoor air.

B.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
B.q: A 58-year-old woman has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic, glaucoma treated with an oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, and heartburn for which she takes a calcium carbonate antacid. Her kidney function has worsened, and serum ketones are negative. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.26 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 23 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 10 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 139 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 101 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which of her medicines best accounts for this blood gas?
opts: Antacids are a cause of saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, which would raise both her pH and her bicarbonate. Her values are both low. Tell: antacid alkalosis shows a bicarbonate above 26, not 10.

A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor causes a normal-gap metabolic acidosis, with a gap within 9 to 15 and a high chloride. Her gap is 28 and her chloride normal, so an elevated-gap cause is needed. Tell: calculate the gap before choosing between the two lists.

Diuretic therapy causes saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, with a high pH and a high bicarbonate. She has a pH of 7.26 and a bicarbonate of 10, the opposite. Tell: a diuretic raises the bicarbonate; hers has fallen.

Correct. Low pH with a low bicarbonate is metabolic acidosis, and the gap is 139 - (101 + 10) = 28, above 9 to 15: elevated. Metformin is one of the elevated-gap causes (the M of the mnemonic), and negative ketones argue against ketoacidosis.

B.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
B.q: Which exacerbation history in the past year places a patient at high exacerbation risk?
opts: No exacerbations is the low-risk row, which places a patient in group A or B depending on symptoms. Tell: high risk needs 2 moderate exacerbations or a hospitalization.
A dyspnea grade of 2 or more
A dyspnea grade of 2 or more means more symptoms, the other axis of the grid. Tell: symptoms decide A versus B, while exacerbations decide high risk. It cannot by itself make a patient high risk.
Cough for 3 months of the year
Cough for 3 months a year is part of the chronic bronchitis definition, not an exacerbation count. Tell: risk is set by exacerbations and hospital admissions in the past year.

Correct. High risk is 2 or more moderate exacerbations, or 1 or more leading to hospital admission, in the past year. Low risk is 0 or 1 exacerbation not leading to admission. High risk moves a patient to group E (or C or D in the 2020 scheme).

B.io: Explain how acid-base disorders affect electrolytes and oxygenation.
B.q: Which electrolyte change may accompany chronic respiratory acidosis?
opts: A high chloride goes with the compensation for respiratory alkalosis (kidneys retain chloride) and with normal-gap metabolic acidosis. Chronic respiratory acidosis lowers chloride. Tell: chloride is lost with ammonium chloride in this disorder.

Correct. In chronic respiratory acidosis the kidneys excrete acid as ammonium chloride, so serum chloride may fall (hypochloremia) while bicarbonate rises. Chloride leaves with the acid the kidney excretes.

Low calcium with tetany belongs to respiratory alkalosis, where a high pH increases calcium binding with albumin. Chronic respiratory acidosis may cause hypochloremia. Tell: tetany points to alkalosis, hypochloremia to chronic respiratory acidosis.

Sodium is not the electrolyte change listed for chronic respiratory acidosis. The renal excretion of acid as ammonium chloride may cause hypochloremia. Tell: the electrolyte that moves is chloride, which leaves in the urine with ammonium.
B.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 25

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: A 31-year-old man with no known tuberculosis risk factors has his tuberculin skin test read at 48 hours. There is 20 mm of erythema around 9 mm of transverse induration. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Negative; 9 mm is below his 15 mm cut-off

Correct. The reader measures transverse induration in millimeters and does not measure erythema. With no known risk factors his cut-off is 15 mm, and his induration is 9 mm, so the result is negative despite the wide redness.
Positive; 9 mm is above a 5 mm cut-off

5 mm is the cut-off for human immunodeficiency virus, recent close contact, transplant, major immunosuppression or imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis. Tell: he has no known risk factors, so his cut-off is 15 mm.
Positive; 20 mm is above his 15 mm cut-off
20 mm is the erythema, and erythema is not measured. Tell: the trained reader compares the 9 mm of induration, not the redness, with his 15 mm cut-off, and 9 mm falls short.
Positive; 20 mm is above a 10 mm cut-off

This makes two errors: it reads the erythema and uses the 10 mm cut-off meant for increased exposure risk, congregate settings or age under 5. Tell: with no risk factors and 9 mm of induration, the result is negative.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: What is the preferred treatment for Pneumocystis pneumonia?
opts: Clindamycin plus primaquine is one of the alternatives chosen by severity when the preferred drug cannot be used, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is checked before primaquine. Tell: first choice is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

Liposomal amphotericin B, with flucytosine, is the induction for severe cryptococcosis. Tell: Pneumocystis, though classed as a fungus, is treated mainly with antibiotics, led by trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.
Intravenous pentamidine is an alternative that depends on severity, not the preferred drug. Tell: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is preferred, intravenous for moderate-to-severe disease and then oral.

Correct. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is preferred, intravenous for moderate-to-severe disease and then oral after improvement, adjusted for renal function. It is also the preferred prophylactic drug.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
B.q: A 66-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes for a routine visit in October. She has not had any vaccines in the past 5 years. Which vaccines are due now?
opts: The yearly influenza vaccine is due, but at 66 she has also passed the age-65 point for the pneumococcal vaccine. Tell: both vaccines are due in a 66-year-old who has had neither.
The pneumococcal vaccine is due at 65, but the yearly influenza shot is the vaccine proven to reduce hospitalizations and death. Tell: it is October, and she needs both.

Correct. Every patient should get a yearly influenza shot, proven to reduce hospitalizations and death, and every patient should receive the pneumococcal vaccine at age 65 to reduce community-acquired pneumonia. At 66 and unvaccinated, she needs both.
Vaccines prevent exacerbations and pneumonia and are given routinely, not after an exacerbation. Tell: yearly influenza and age-65 pneumococcal vaccination are both due now.

B.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
B.q: A 47-year-old woman has a metabolic alkalosis with normal blood pressure; she denies vomiting, diuretics and antacids. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 46 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 32 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which test separates the saline-responsive from the saline-unresponsive type?
opts: The Winter formula predicts the carbon dioxide in metabolic acidosis; it does not type an alkalosis. Tell: Winter checks compensation in acidosis only.

Correct. Urine chloride differentiates the two types: it is low (below 25 mEq/L) in saline-responsive alkalosis and high (above 40 mEq/L) in saline-unresponsive alkalosis. Her history gives no obvious cause, so the test sorts the list.
The anion gap sorts metabolic acidosis into normal and elevated gap; it does not type an alkalosis. Tell: anion gap for acidosis, urine chloride for alkalosis.
Albumin matters for interpreting the anion gap, since low albumin lowers it. It does not split saline-responsive from unresponsive alkalosis. Tell: albumin goes with the gap.
