C.q: What does nursing-home residence alone mean for the choice of pneumonia antibiotics?
opts: Hospital-acquired pneumonia is defined by timing, 48 hours or more after admission. Tell: a nursing-home resident who develops pneumonia before admission has community-acquired pneumonia.
It does not mandate broad-spectrum therapy

Correct. The healthcare-associated pneumonia category is retired: nursing-home residence or healthcare exposure alone does not mandate broad-spectrum therapy. Prior respiratory isolation of resistant organisms and recent hospitalization with intravenous antibiotics are assessed instead.

Residence does not set duration. Nonsevere community-acquired pneumonia may use fewer than 5 days (minimum 3), severe at least 5. Tell: duration follows severity and response, not where the patient lives.

Resistant-pathogen coverage is added only for validated risks, such as prior respiratory isolation of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas. Tell: residence alone is not one of them.

C.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
C.q: A 70-year-old man with hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic is light-headed on standing. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.49 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 46 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 34 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); potassium 3.2 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L); urine chloride is low. Along with isotonic saline, which medication change is indicated?
opts: Antacids are a cause of saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, so starting one adds alkali to an alkalemia. Tell: antacid, diuretic and vomiting sit together on the cause list.
Mineralocorticoids cause a hypertensive, saline-unresponsive metabolic alkalosis, so adding one would worsen his. Tell: mineralocorticoids are on the cause list, not the treatment list.
A second diuretic would deepen the volume contraction and the alkalosis; diuretics are discontinued in saline-responsive alkalosis. Tell: the drug causing the alkalosis is stopped, not doubled.

Correct. Low urine chloride and orthostatic symptoms mark a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, and diuretic therapy is a listed cause. Treatment is isotonic saline for the volume deficit and discontinuing the diuretic.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
C.q: A 51-year-old man has 5 weeks of cough, night sweats and weight loss, and pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected. Which sputum collection plan is appropriate?
opts: Two samples, collected 1 hour apart in clinic
Two specimens an hour apart are too few and too close together. Tell: the plan is 3 specimens 8 to 24 hours apart, with at least one early-morning specimen.
One sample, collected at any time of day
A single specimen falls short of the 3 specimens required, and timing matters. Tell: collect 3 specimens 8 to 24 hours apart, with at least one taken early in the morning.
Three samples, 1 each week for 3 weeks
Three is the right number, but specimens are collected 8 to 24 hours apart, not a week apart. Tell: the whole set is collected within a few days, with at least one early-morning specimen.
Three samples 8 to 24 hours apart, 1 early morning

Correct. Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis calls for 3 sputum specimens collected 8 to 24 hours apart, with at least one early-morning specimen, sent for acid-fast smear and mycobacterial culture, with a rapid molecular test on at least one.

C.io: Describe the major buffer systems of the body.
C.q: A 60-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis is hypoventilating, and her carbon dioxide is rising. Following water + carbon dioxide <-> carbonic acid <-> hydrogen ion + bicarbonate, what happens to her hydrogen ion concentration?
opts: Correct. Added carbon dioxide drives the carbonic acid reaction to the right, forming more carbonic acid and then more hydrogen ion and bicarbonate, so pH falls: hypoventilation, raised carbon dioxide, acidemia.
Falling hydrogen ion follows a fall in carbon dioxide, as in hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. Her carbon dioxide is rising. Tell: more carbon dioxide means more acid.
It rises once the kidneys respond
The hydrogen ion rises as soon as carbon dioxide rises; the kidneys respond later (6 to 12 hours) by retaining bicarbonate to blunt it. Tell: the chemistry is immediate; the renal response is slow.
It is unchanged; bicarbonate absorbs it

Bicarbonate is formed alongside the hydrogen ion in this reaction; it does not cancel it, and the pH falls. Compensation never fully corrects the pH. Tell: both products of the reaction rise together.

Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
C.q: A 24-year-old woman with asthma has had fever, myalgias, cough and a sore throat for 30 hours, and influenza is confirmed by molecular testing. She is well enough for outpatient care. Which antiviral should be avoided?
opts: Correct. Inhaled zanamivir is avoided in asthma and chronic obstructive lung disease because of the risk of bronchospasm. Her asthma makes it the antiviral to avoid; oseltamivir, single-dose baloxavir within 48 hours, or intravenous peramivir remain options for uncomplicated outpatient influenza.

Oseltamivir is the preferred influenza antiviral, including for high-risk patients, and asthma is no reason to avoid it. Tell: the antiviral with a breathing-specific warning is the inhaled one, zanamivir, because of bronchospasm.

Intravenous peramivir is an option for eligible outpatients with uncomplicated influenza, with renal dose adjustment. Her asthma is irrelevant to an intravenous drug. Tell: bronchospasm risk belongs to the inhaled route.

Single-dose baloxavir is an option for uncomplicated influenza within 48 hours in eligible patients aged 5 or older; she is 24, at 30 hours, and not pregnant. Tell: asthma restricts the inhaled antiviral, not baloxavir.

C.topic: Reading the fraction from the flow
C.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
C.q: A 57-year-old man with bronchitis is placed on a simple mask at 6 to 7 L/min. About what fraction of inspired oxygen is he receiving?
opts: 28% is a nasal cannula value at 2 L/min. A simple mask at 6 to 7 L/min delivers more, and the listed value for that flow is 40%. Tell: 28% is a low cannula setting; the mask is higher.

Correct. A simple mask is a low flow device set at 5-10 L/min, and its fraction depends on the flow: 5-6 L/min gives 35%, 6-7 L/min gives 40%, and 7-8 L/min gives 50%. At 6 to 7 L/min he is receiving about 40%.
50% is the simple mask's value at 7-8 L/min, one step higher than his setting. His 6 to 7 L/min corresponds to 40%. Tell: match the flow row; each row steps up by 5 or 10 points.
80% is far above a simple mask's range of 35-50%. Those values belong to higher-flow, reservoir-bag devices such as the non-rebreather mask at 10-15 L/min. Tell: a simple mask cannot approach 80%.

C.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
C.q: A 27-year-old man describes cough and chest tightness with cold air and smoke over several months. His spirometry is normal, with no meaningful change after albuterol. Asthma is still suspected. Which test is most appropriate next?
opts: An exercise challenge is the provocation test used when exercise-induced bronchospasm is suspected. His triggers are cold air and smoke, not exercise. Tell: for a nondiagnostic spirometry with general triggers, methacholine or histamine challenge is the test.
ruled out by a stated finding

Annual spirometry is for monitoring the progression of known disease, not for settling a suspected diagnosis today. Tell: when spirometry is not diagnostic, bronchial provocation testing is the next test.

Correct. Bronchial provocation testing with methacholine or histamine is useful when spirometry is not diagnostic, as here, where a typical history meets normal spirometry. His normal lung function also clears the rule that provocation is not done below 65% predicted.

The chest x-ray in asthma is usually normal or shows hyperinflation, so it adds little after normal spirometry. Tell: when spirometry fails to show asthma, the next step is to provoke airway hyper-responsiveness with methacholine.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
C.q: During an asthma attack, a patient is using accessory muscles and leaning forward, yet no wheezing is heard. What does the missing wheeze most likely indicate?
opts: A silent chest in a patient still working hard to breathe does not mean the attack is over. Wheezing can vanish in severe exacerbations, leaving only decreased breath sounds. Tell: improvement brings easier breathing as well as less wheeze, not a struggling patient with a quiet chest.
A cardiac cause of the attack

Cardiac asthma causes wheezing from heart failure, so it would add wheeze rather than remove it. In a severe asthma exacerbation, wheezing may be absent, leaving only decreased breath sounds. Tell: the quiet chest is explained by the severity of the attack, not by the heart.

Beta-2 agonist side effects are tremor and palpitations, not loss of wheeze. In a severe exacerbation, wheezing may be absent, leaving only decreased breath sounds with prolonged expiration. Tell: drug side effects show in the pulse and hands, while a quiet chest belongs to the severe attack itself.

Correct. Accessory muscle use and leaning forward show increased work of breathing, and wheezing may not be present in a severe exacerbation; the patient may have only decreased breath sounds with a prolonged expiratory phase. A quiet chest in a struggling patient signals severity, not improvement.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
C.q: A 46-year-old woman has new-onset persistent wheezing and cough that began last year. She has nasal polyps. Allergy skin tests are negative and her serum immunoglobulin E is normal. She had a wheezing episode after taking aspirin for a headache. Which type of asthma is most likely?
opts: Correct. Adult onset, persistent symptoms, nasal polyps, negative skin tests with a normal immunoglobulin E, and aspirin sensitivity all fit intrinsic asthma, the non-atopic form seen in about 10% of patients, which is usually more severe and persistent.

Extrinsic asthma is allergen-triggered and atopic, so skin tests would be positive and immunoglobulin E raised. Her tests are negative and immunoglobulin E normal. Tell: negative allergy testing rules out the allergic, extrinsic form.
ruled out by a stated finding

Catamenial asthma is timed to predictable points of the menstrual cycle, and her history gives no cyclic pattern. Tell: her clues are polyps, adult onset and an aspirin reaction, the intrinsic profile, not a monthly rhythm.

Occupational asthma follows workplace sensitization and improves on weekends and vacations; nothing in her history points to work. Tell: polyps, aspirin sensitivity and negative allergy tests describe intrinsic asthma, while occupational asthma is defined by its work pattern.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
C.q: A 68-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a resting oxygen saturation of 93%, but during a walking test she drops to 85%. She is mobile and reports exertional breathlessness. Which oxygen plan is indicated?
opts: Her drop to 85% while walking is severe exertional desaturation, which qualifies for oxygen during exertion. Tell: a normal-looking resting value does not rule out an exertional indication.

Correct. Severe exertional desaturation, 88% or less with exertion, qualifies for long-term oxygen during exertion. Her resting saturation of 93% is moderate desaturation, without a resting indication, so oxygen is used with activity.
Oxygen for more than 15 hours a day requires severe resting desaturation, 88% or less at rest. She is 93% at rest. Tell: her drop happens with exertion, so oxygen is given during exertion.
ruled out by a stated finding
Night-only desaturation leads to an evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea, and her drop happens while walking. Tell: oxygen should match the setting where she desaturates, exertion.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
C.q: A 55-year-old woman with group B chronic obstructive pulmonary disease still smokes a pack a day. She asks what single step would do the most to slow her disease. Which intervention is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Smoking cessation is the only treatment that can slow progression, and every attempt should be combined with counseling to increase efficacy; nicotine replacement, bupropion or varenicline can be added. It is essential for every group.

An inhaled corticosteroid adds pneumonia risk and must be combined with a long-acting beta agonist and raises pneumonia risk. Tell: no inhaler is the step that most helps survival; stopping smoking is.
Chest computed tomography can categorize emphysema but is generally not needed, and imaging changes nothing about progression. Tell: her most powerful step is quitting smoking with counseling.
Long-term azithromycin is not among the measures listed for improving survival. Tell: the intervention with a survival benefit is smoking cessation.

C.io: Identify and discuss vaccines which prevent respiratory infections.
C.q: A 34-year-old woman who smokes cigarettes and has type 1 diabetes has never received a pneumococcal vaccine. Which vaccine plan is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Adults aged 19 to 49 with a qualifying risk condition and no prior conjugate vaccine are vaccinated, and cigarette smoking and diabetes mellitus are both listed risk conditions. One 20-valent or 21-valent conjugate dose completes her series.

Adult Hib vaccination is used only for selected indications, such as asplenia without prior vaccination or after stem-cell transplant. She has neither. Tell: smoking and diabetes are pneumococcal risk conditions, not Hib indications.
Age 50 is when every adult qualifies, but adults 19 to 49 with a risk condition qualify now. She has two, smoking and diabetes. Tell: risk conditions bring pneumococcal vaccination forward.

Respiratory syncytial virus vaccine is one dose for adults aged 75 or older and adults 50 to 74 at increased risk. At 34 she is too young. Tell: her age and conditions match the pneumococcal recommendation instead.

C.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
C.q: A 58-year-old man with chronic kidney failure who has missed several dialysis sessions is nauseated and fatigued. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.26 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 29 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 13 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 100 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: His carbon dioxide is low, but his pH of 7.26 is acidemia. A low carbon dioxide with a low pH is compensation for the metabolic acidosis, not a primary alkalosis. Tell: alkalosis requires a high pH.

The gap is 138 - (100 + 13) = 25, above 15, so it is elevated, not normal. A normal-gap acidosis would have a gap within 9 to 15 and a high chloride, and his chloride of 100 is normal. Tell: do the subtraction before choosing the gap type.
ruled out by a stated finding
Respiratory acidosis needs a high carbon dioxide, and his is 29. The low bicarbonate of 13 matches the acidemia. Tell: a low carbon dioxide with a low bicarbonate means the lungs are compensating.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. The pH of 7.26 is acidemia, and the bicarbonate of 13 is low and matches it: metabolic. Gap = 138 - (100 + 13) = 25, above 9 to 15, so it is elevated; uremia is an elevated-gap cause. The carbon dioxide of 29 is compensation (Winter 1.5 x 13 + 8 = 27.5, plus or minus 2).
C.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 55

C.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
C.q: A 36-year-old woman with moderate persistent asthma was given salmeterol by itself at an urgent care visit and it has been her sole controller for a month. Which change does her regimen need?
opts: Cromolyn is a mast cell stabilizer for prevention in mild persistent or exercise-induced asthma. Swapping it in still leaves her without the preferred anti-inflammatory controller. Tell: the missing piece is the inhaled corticosteroid.

Tiotropium, an anticholinergic, is less effective than beta-2 agonists, slow in onset, and not an anti-inflammatory. Tell: her problem is a bronchodilator used without the inhaled corticosteroid it must be paired with.

Correct. A long-acting beta-2 agonist such as salmeterol has no anti-inflammatory effect and should not be used as monotherapy; it is used in combination with an inhaled corticosteroid. Adding one treats her airway inflammation and may allow control at a lower steroid dose.

Salmeterol bronchodilates for up to 12 hours, but it has no anti-inflammatory effect, and monotherapy is specifically warned against. Tell: the combination with an inhaled corticosteroid is what makes a long-acting beta-2 agonist appropriate.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
C.q: A 45-year-old woman without asthma or chronic lung disease has 8 days of cough after a cold, with a mild expiratory wheeze. She is afebrile with a normal oxygen saturation and no focal findings. Which treatment should not be prescribed routinely?
opts: A short bronchodilator trial may help selected patients with wheeze or airflow obstruction, and she has a wheeze; it is reasonable, with reassessment for asthma if it persists. Tell: bronchodilators are allowed for wheeze; the steroid is the routine prescription to avoid.

Correct. Systemic or inhaled corticosteroids are not routinely prescribed for uncomplicated bronchitis. Her wheeze is the transient wheeze of bronchitis from inflammation and mucus, with no asthma history and no focal findings, so a steroid adds risk without benefit.

Acetaminophen is a reasonable option for fever or discomfort, with a check that no combination product duplicates it. Tell: it is a symptom-relief measure, not one of the routine prescriptions the bronchitis guidance warns against.

Explaining the expected course is part of management: the cough commonly lasts 2 to 3 weeks and may persist longer. Tell: counseling is what replaces unnecessary prescriptions, so it is the step to keep, not the one to withhold.

C.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
C.q: A 21-year-old man with extrinsic asthma flares whenever he cleans his apartment, and allergy skin testing shows sensitivity to house dust mites. His controller and rescue inhalers are prescribed. Which non-drug measure should be added?
opts: Move from the city to a rural area
Moving is not a listed measure; trigger avoidance and environmental control are. Tell: his identified trigger is dust mites inside his home, so environmental control there is the measure.

Exercise is a listed trigger, but asthma treatment aims for no limitation on physical activity, so cutting activity is not the measure. Tell: his trigger, shown by skin testing and cleaning flares, is dust mites, so avoidance targets the home.

Immunotherapy may be considered for allergic triggers, but it must be done in a controlled environment because it can induce bronchoconstriction. Tell: home use is unsafe, and the first non-drug step is avoiding the dust mite trigger.
Reduce dust mite exposure at home

Correct. Non-pharmacological asthma treatment is trigger avoidance and environmental control. Dust mites are the most common inhaled allergen trigger, and his skin test and cleaning-related flares identify it, so reducing his exposure at home is the added measure.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for respiratory infections in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
C.q: An 84-year-old woman with dysphagia after a stroke is recovering from aspiration pneumonia on a general ward. Which measure best addresses her risk of another episode?
opts: Correct. After aspiration pneumonia, assess swallowing, oral hygiene, positioning and reversible risks, and address recurrent aspiration risk. Dysphagia is a listed risk factor, so a swallowing assessment targets the cause of her aspiration.

Antibiotics treat established infection, and prophylactic antibiotics are avoided when bacterial infection is not suspected. Tell: recurrence is prevented by fixing the aspiration risk (swallowing, oral hygiene, positioning), not by continuous antibiotics.

Positioning is one of the risks to assess and correct after aspiration, and the proper positioning named for ventilated patients is head of bed elevated, not flat. Tell: the measure should lower the chance of colonized material reaching the lung.

Routine chest physiotherapy is described as not essential even in lung abscess care, and it does nothing about the swallowing problem that let her aspirate. Tell: prevention targets dysphagia, oral hygiene and positioning.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
C.q: A 36-year-old woman with human immunodeficiency virus infection starts trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis pneumonia. Her arterial oxygen pressure on room air is 61 mm Hg. Which therapy should be added?
opts: Pentamidine is an alternative to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, not an add-on for low oxygen. Deterioration is reassessed for toxicity, coinfection or failure rather than met with an automatic switch. Tell: her oxygen value triggers a steroid, not a second antimicrobial.

The adjunct is a systemic corticosteroid, prednisone, given over 21 days; an inhaled steroid does not provide it. Tell: the room-air oxygen below 70 mm Hg calls for systemic prednisone started early, not an inhaler.

Correct. Adjunctive corticosteroids are indicated in Pneumocystis pneumonia linked to human immunodeficiency virus when the room-air arterial oxygen pressure is below 70 mm Hg, and hers is 61. Prednisone is started as early as possible, ideally within 72 hours of starting treatment.

Her room-air arterial oxygen pressure of 61 mm Hg is below the threshold of 70, which is exactly when adjunctive steroids are indicated. Tell: compare the stated value with 70 mm Hg; below it, a steroid is added as early as possible.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
C.q: An 82-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease takes 9 medicines, several of which have anticholinergic effects. Her clinician is considering adding tiotropium, a long-acting antimuscarinic. Which pharmacology concern is heightened at her age?
opts: Correct. Pharmacology concerns in older adults include polypharmacy, anticholinergic burden, cardiac effects of long-acting beta agonists, and inhaled corticosteroid-related pneumonia and fracture risk. Adding an antimuscarinic to several anticholinergic medicines raises that burden.
Pneumonia risk is tied to inhaled corticosteroids, not to tiotropium. Tell: an antimuscarinic added to other anticholinergic medicines raises anticholinergic burden.
Arrhythmias and worsening atrial fibrillation are concerns with long-acting beta agonists. Tell: tiotropium is an antimuscarinic, so the concern is anticholinergic burden.

Oral corticosteroids are for acute exacerbations only in this disease and are not part of the plan being considered. Tell: tiotropium is an antimuscarinic, so adding it to her anticholinergic medicines raises anticholinergic burden.
ruled out by a stated finding

C.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
C.q: A 66-year-old man on home oxygen restores old cars in his garage and rubs grease off his hands with an oil-based cleanser while wearing his cannula. Which teaching applies?
opts: Turn the flow up while working

Turning the flow up does not remove the petroleum product; the teaching is to avoid petroleum-based oils and grease, not to change the flow. Tell: the fix is to change the product, not the oxygen setting.
Wear a simple mask in the garage

A simple mask is a low flow device for mild to moderate respiratory distress. He has no respiratory problem described, and changing the mask would not address the grease. Tell: his hazard is the product on his hands.

Correct. Home oxygen teaching is to avoid petroleum-based products such as lip balms, lotions, oils and grease. He is wearing his cannula while rubbing grease off with an oil-based cleanser, so he should avoid those petroleum oils and grease.
Use a Venturi mask when working

A Venturi mask is a high flow device that gives a precise fraction, often used in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It would not remove the petroleum product hazard. Tell: the teaching concerns what touches the oxygen, not which mask he wears.

C.io: Select the appropriate equipment and supplies necessary for initiating oxygen therapy.
C.q: A 72-year-old man with a long-term tracheostomy after head and neck cancer needs humidified supplemental oxygen at home. Which interface delivers air-entrainment nebulizer oxygen to his airway?
opts: An open face mask is an air-entrainment nebulizer interface, but it sits over the face, as does the aerosol mask. A man who breathes through a tracheostomy needs the interface that fits the stoma. Tell: face interfaces are the aerosol and open face masks; the stoma interface is the trach collar.

A nasal cannula sits in the nostrils, which would not reach a patient breathing through a tracheostomy, and it is a low flow device, not an air-entrainment one. Tell: the cannula is a nose device; the trach collar is the tracheostomy device.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. He has a long-term tracheostomy and needs humidified oxygen delivered by an air-entrainment nebulizer. The trach collar is the air-entrainment nebulizer interface that fits over a tracheostomy, so it delivers to his airway directly.

A simple mask is a low flow device that covers the nose and mouth. It is not an air-entrainment nebulizer interface, and it would sit over a stoma he breathes through. Tell: the simple mask is a face interface with a variable fraction; the trach collar is the airway interface on this system.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
D.q: A 54-year-old man with severe pneumonia is on an aerosol mask from an air-entrainment nebulizer. The team wants to raise its fraction to 0.80. Why is that setting a concern?
opts: It changes with his breathing rate

An air-entrainment system gives a fixed fraction that does not fluctuate with patient demand. A fraction that follows breathing rate describes the cannula, simple mask or non-rebreather. Tell: air entrainment is steady; the concern with 0.80 is the recommended ceiling.
This device is not capped at 0.28. It can deliver higher fractions, and the concern is the specific recommendation not to go above 0.50. Tell: the limit is a recommended ceiling of 0.50, not 0.28.
The recommendation is the opposite: use above 0.50 is not recommended. Reading it as recommended would invert the ceiling. Tell: 0.50 is a ceiling, not a floor.

Correct. A fixed-fraction air-entrainment nebulizer can deliver higher fractions, but setting above 0.50 is not recommended. His team wants 0.80, which is beyond that ceiling, so it is a concern even though his pneumonia is severe.

D.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
D.q: A 69-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease says that, walking on level ground, he has to stop for breath after about 100 meters or after a few minutes. Which modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade fits?
opts: Grade 1 is shortness of breath when hurrying on the level or walking up a slight hill. Tell: he stops on level ground after about 100 meters, a heavier limitation.
Grade 2 is walking slower than people of the same age on the level, or stopping for breath at one's own pace. Tell: a defined stop at about 100 meters or a few minutes is grade 3.

Correct. Grade 3 is stopping for breath after walking about 100 meters or after a few minutes on the level. A grade of 2 or more counts as more symptoms, which places him in group B or E depending on exacerbation risk.
Grade 4 is being too breathless to leave the house, or breathless when dressing or undressing. Tell: he still walks outside, stopping after 100 meters, which is grade 3.

D.io: Define, describe, and discuss aspergillosis as it relates to asthma.
D.q: A 29-year-old man with long-standing asthma has had several exacerbations this year despite good inhaler technique and compliance. Testing shows a strong hypersensitivity to Aspergillus fumigatus with markedly raised immunoglobulin E and immunoglobulin G antibodies to the mold. Which diagnosis explains his worsening?
opts: Non-compliance is the most common reason for poor control, but the stem states good technique and compliance. Tell: once compliance is confirmed, the antibody response to Aspergillus is the stated explanation for his exacerbations.
ruled out by a stated finding

Steroid-resistant asthma is very uncommon, and nothing here shows a failed steroid response. His specific antibody response to Aspergillus explains the exacerbations. Tell: a named mold with raised immunoglobulin E and G points to aspergillosis, not to drug resistance.

Correct. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus that occurs almost exclusively in asthma or cystic fibrosis; exposure causes a vigorous immunoglobulin E and G response that produces acute asthma symptoms and exacerbations, as in this patient.

Occupational asthma comes from workplace chemicals and improves away from work. His trigger is an identified mold with a vigorous antibody response. Tell: the stem names Aspergillus and the antibodies, the hallmark of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

D.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
D.q: A 31-year-old woman has spirometry for suspected asthma. Before a bronchodilator her forced expiratory volume in 1 second is 61% predicted with a ratio of 55%; after albuterol it is 94% predicted, a 54% improvement. Which interpretation fits?
opts: Correct. A reduced 1-second volume and a reduced ratio before the bronchodilator show airflow limitation, and a 54% improvement after albuterol, far above the 12% threshold, shows reversibility. A positive bronchodilator response strongly supports asthma.

Spirometry does depend on effort, and coaching helps, but poor effort would not produce a clear 54% rise after a bronchodilator. Tell: a large, consistent response to albuterol reflects reversible obstruction, not inconsistent effort.

Fixed obstruction would barely change after a bronchodilator. Her 1-second volume rose by 54% of its starting value, from 61% to 94% predicted. Tell: a rise of 12% or more is the reversible pattern that supports asthma.

Before the bronchodilator her 1-second volume was 61% predicted with a 55% ratio, both reduced, so the test is not normal. Tell: the pre-bronchodilator values show obstruction, and the post-bronchodilator values show it reversing.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.topic: Flow rates and fraction of inspired oxygen
D.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
D.q: Above what fraction of inspired oxygen is an air-entrainment nebulizer not recommended?
opts: 0.30 is below the recommended limit, which is not recommended above 0.50. At 0.30 the device would be used well within its recommended range. Tell: the ceiling is 0.50.
Correct. An air-entrainment nebulizer can deliver higher fractions of inspired oxygen, but use above 0.50 is not recommended. The recommended ceiling is 0.50, which corresponds to 50%.
0.80 is above the recommended ceiling. The device can deliver higher fractions, but use above 0.50 is not recommended. Tell: the recommended limit is 0.50, not 0.80.
1.0 is the top of the printed range for this device, not the recommended ceiling. Delivery above 0.50 is not recommended. Tell: the device can reach high fractions but is not recommended above 0.50.

D.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
D.q: A 28-year-old pregnant woman with allergic asthma asks whether keeping her baby away from dust, pets and pollen will prevent the child from developing asthma. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Avoidance matters just for pet dander
No single allergen is singled out; allergen avoidance in general does not reduce the risk of developing asthma. Tell: avoidance controls triggers in someone who has asthma, but does not prevent it.
Avoidance does not lower the risk

Correct. Inhaled allergens are common triggers and are implicated in sensitization, but avoiding allergens does not reduce the risk of developing asthma, and early exposure may even be protective by building tolerance.
Early exposure may be protective through tolerance, and not all atopic individuals develop asthma. Tell: exposure early in life is not a cause the evidence supports avoiding.

Avoiding allergens does not reduce the risk of developing asthma, so strict avoidance is not prevention. Tell: early exposure may be protective through tolerance, the opposite of what strict avoidance assumes.

Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
D.q: A 68-year-old woman is admitted for repair of a hip fracture. On hospital day 4 she develops fever, purulent sputum and a new infiltrate that was not on her admission chest radiograph. She has not been intubated. How should this pneumonia be classified?
opts: Aspiration pneumonitis is a sterile chemical injury with abrupt decline after a witnessed aspiration, and fever can occur without infection. No aspiration event is described, and she has purulent sputum with a new infiltrate. Tell: pneumonitis follows a witnessed event within hours.

Community-acquired pneumonia is acquired outside the hospital or present early in admission. Hers began on day 4 after a clear admission film. Tell: an infiltrate that appears 48 hours or more into the stay is hospital acquired.
ruled out by a stated finding

Ventilator-associated pneumonia develops more than 48 hours after endotracheal intubation, and she has never been intubated. Tell: without a breathing tube there is no ventilator-associated label, however long the stay.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Hospital-acquired pneumonia develops 48 hours or more after admission and was not incubating on admission. Her new infiltrate appeared on day 4 after a clear admission film, and she was never intubated, so the ventilator label does not apply.

D.io: Identify compensatory mechanisms for simple acid-base disorders.
D.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic lung disease has been vomiting for days. His bicarbonate is 40 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L), his pH 7.46 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), and his carbon dioxide 58 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg). What does the carbon dioxide level indicate?
opts: Compensation for metabolic alkalosis rarely takes carbon dioxide above 55, and his 58 is past that limit, so compensation alone does not explain it. Tell: the 55 ceiling separates compensation from a second disorder.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. In metabolic alkalosis, respiratory compensation rarely raises carbon dioxide above 55 mm Hg. His 58 is above that (and above 52, the 16 x 0.75 rise from 40), so a concurrent primary respiratory acidosis fits, along with his chronic lung disease.

A respiratory alkalosis would lower carbon dioxide, and his is 58, which is high. The excess points to a concurrent respiratory acidosis. Tell: respiratory alkalosis would pull carbon dioxide below normal.

His bicarbonate is 40 and his pH 7.46, both on the alkaline side, so there is no metabolic acidosis. The high carbon dioxide suggests an added respiratory acidosis. Tell: a metabolic acidosis would lower the bicarbonate.
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 38

D.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
D.q: A 26-year-old woman has asthma symptoms only 1 day a week and uses albuterol 1 day a week, but she wakes at night with cough twice a week. She has no activity limitation, and her forced expiratory volume in 1 second is 86% predicted. Which severity classification fits?
opts: Her daytime symptoms, rescue use and 86% function would fit intermittent, but severity follows the worst feature, and waking twice a week exceeds the intermittent limit of 2 or fewer times a month. Tell: one moderate feature outranks several mild ones.

Mild persistent asthma allows night waking 3 to 4 times a month. She wakes twice a week, which is more than once a week, the moderate persistent level. Tell: twice weekly is roughly 8 times a month, past the mild limit.

Correct. Severity is assigned to the most severe category in which any feature occurs. Her daytime symptoms and lung function are intermittent-level, but night awakenings more than once a week (twice weekly) are a moderate persistent feature, so she is moderate persistent.

Severe persistent asthma brings waking often 7 times a week with symptoms throughout the day and function under 60%. She wakes twice a week with 86% function. Tell: her worst feature reaches moderate, not severe.

D.topic: Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap
D.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
D.q: Which chloride pattern goes with normal anion gap metabolic acidosis?
opts: Normochloremia goes with the elevated-gap type, where unmeasured anions replace bicarbonate. The normal-gap type is hyperchloremic. Tell: normal chloride means unmeasured anions, high chloride means a normal gap.
Correct. Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis is hyperchloremic, since chloride rises as bicarbonate falls. Elevated anion gap acidosis is normochloremic, because other anions replace the bicarbonate.
Chloride does change: in normal-gap acidosis it rises (hyperchloremic) to balance the lost bicarbonate. Tell: the key finding is a high chloride with a low bicarbonate.
Low chloride appears in metabolic alkalosis and chronic respiratory acidosis. Normal-gap acidosis is hyperchloremic. Tell: low chloride goes with alkalosis states.
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 52

D.io: Identify and discuss vaccines which prevent respiratory infections.
D.q: A 55-year-old man with no medical conditions has never received a pneumococcal vaccine. Which pneumococcal vaccination is appropriate for him?
opts: Pneumococcal vaccination is recommended for all adults aged 50 or older who have not had a conjugate vaccine. At 55 he already qualifies. Tell: the age threshold is 50, not 65.

A 15-valent conjugate vaccine usually needs the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine afterward, so by itself it leaves the series incomplete. Tell: a single dose completes the series only with the 20-valent or 21-valent conjugate vaccine.

Pneumococcal vaccination is a series completed by one 20-valent or 21-valent conjugate dose, not an annual vaccine. Tell: the yearly vaccine is influenza; the pneumococcal series is done once completed.

Correct. All adults aged 50 or older who have never had a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, or whose history is unknown, are vaccinated. One dose of the 20-valent or 21-valent conjugate vaccine completes the series; a 15-valent conjugate vaccine is usually followed by the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: A 64-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a symptom assessment test score of 17 and a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 2. She has had no exacerbations in the past year. Which initial maintenance regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. A score of 17 and a dyspnea grade of 2 mean more symptoms, and no exacerbations means low risk, which is group B. Group B starts on a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic, ideally in a single inhaler for convenience.
One bronchodilator is the start for group A, with fewer symptoms. Her score of 17 and dyspnea grade of 2 put her in group B. Tell: more symptoms call for both long-acting bronchodilators.

An inhaled corticosteroid adds pneumonia risk and is considered in group E with eosinophils of 300 or more. She is group B, low risk. Tell: group B's start is the 2 long-acting bronchodilators, without a steroid.
Long-term azithromycin is used rarely and increases resistance and side effects. Tell: a symptomatic, low-risk patient starts on dual long-acting bronchodilators.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
D.q: What is the most common pathogen in community-acquired pneumonia?
opts: Correct. Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is the most common pathogen in community-acquired pneumonia. It is the usual cause of lobar pneumonia on the radiograph, and empiric therapy for community-acquired pneumonia covers it.
Klebsiella pneumoniae is linked with alcohol abuse and is a gram-negative cause of pneumonia, but it is not the most common pathogen. Tell: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae is an atypical pathogen, more likely in children and young adults, though it can cause pneumonia in adults. Tell: the single most common pathogen overall is the pneumococcus.

Haemophilus influenzae is one of the community-acquired pneumonia pathogens, linked with smoking and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, but it is not the most common. Tell: pneumococcus leads the list.

D.q: A 59-year-old man with alcoholism and chronic liver disease has community-acquired pneumonia and is stable for outpatient treatment. He had anaphylaxis to amoxicillin in the past. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Amoxicillin by itself is for outpatients with no comorbidities, and he has alcoholism and liver disease as well as an amoxicillin allergy. Tell: two separate clues rule this option out.
ruled out by a stated finding

Doxycycline by itself is for outpatients without comorbidities. His alcoholism and chronic liver disease call for a combination or a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Tell: with comorbidities, doxycycline only partners a beta-lactam.

This is a comorbidity regimen, but amoxicillin-clavulanate contains the amoxicillin that caused his anaphylaxis. Tell: allergy history is reviewed first, and it removes this combination, so the respiratory fluoroquinolone is the remaining listed option.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Alcoholism and chronic liver disease are listed comorbidities, so he needs a beta-lactam plus azithromycin or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin). His amoxicillin anaphylaxis removes the amoxicillin-based combination, leaving the fluoroquinolone, with a review of QT, interactions and fluoroquinolone risks.

D.q: A 57-year-old man with cough and weight loss has a chest radiograph showing an upper-lobe infiltrate with cavitation. What does this radiograph establish?
opts: Latent infection usually has a normal chest radiograph and no symptoms. Tell: a cavitating infiltrate in a man with cough and weight loss suggests disease, which must be confirmed microbiologically.

Correct. Possible radiographic findings include infiltrates, cavities, nodules, adenopathy or effusion, and post-primary disease often involves the upper lobes and may cavitate. But imaging supports suspicion and cannot confirm tuberculosis or reliably determine activity; sputum microbiology is required.

Radiographs cannot reliably distinguish recent infection, reactivation or reinfection, even though post-primary disease often involves the upper lobes. Tell: the film raises suspicion; it does not date the infection.

An upper-lobe cavity raises suspicion, but imaging cannot confirm tuberculosis, and lung cancer, lung abscess and other infections also cause cavitary disease. Tell: confirmation comes from sputum smear, culture and molecular testing.

D.q: A 34-year-old man has newly diagnosed drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis. Which regimen is the standard treatment?
opts: Daily rifampin for 4 months is a latent-infection regimen. Tell: disease needs four drugs (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol) for 2 months, then two for 4.
Isoniazid for 6 or 9 months is a latent-infection alternative when rifamycin regimens are unsuitable. Tell: disease is treated with four drugs first, then two.
Two drugs for 2 months, then four for 4
This reverses the phases: the four-drug phase comes first, for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin continue for 4. Tell: start broad, then narrow.
Four drugs for 2 months, then two for 4

Correct. The standard drug-susceptible regimen is isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for the initial 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months, given daily with directly observed or video-observed therapy to support completion.

D.q: A 36-year-old pet-shop employee has had a week of fever, severe headache, photophobia and a nonproductive cough. Several parakeets in the shop were sick last month. His pulse is 72/min with a temperature of 103°F, his spleen is palpable, and macular rashes on his face resemble the rose spots of typhoid fever (Horder spots). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Histoplasmosis follows inhaled soil or bird or bat droppings and causes fever, chills, myalgias, dry cough and headache. It does not produce relative bradycardia, splenomegaly or Horder spots. Tell: the facial rash and slow pulse belong to psittacosis.

Mycoplasma causes gradual fever, persistent cough and headache, often in school-age children and young adults in group outbreaks. It has no bird exposure link and no Horder spots. Tell: sick birds plus facial rose-spot rashes point to Chlamydia psittaci.

Correct. Psittacosis is an occupational infection of pet-shop and zoo employees and poultry workers, caught from birds such as parakeets. Severe headache, photophobia, a dry cough, relative bradycardia, splenomegaly and Horder spots (facial macular rashes like typhoid rose spots) complete the picture.

Influenza begins suddenly with fever, myalgias, sore throat and a frontal or retro-orbital headache, usually with tachycardia from fever or hypoxia. His pulse is slow for his fever. Tell: relative bradycardia, splenomegaly and Horder spots point away from influenza.

D.q: A 22-year-old college athlete with gastroenteritis has vomited for three days and is dizzy on standing. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.51 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 48 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 37 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); potassium 3.1 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L); urine chloride is low. In addition to treating the cause, which therapy is indicated?
opts: Diuretic therapy is a cause of saline-responsive alkalosis, and diuretics are stopped, not started, in this disorder. He needs volume, not more volume loss. Tell: discontinuing diuretics is part of the treatment.

Breathing into a paper bag is not necessary even for hyperventilation: it fails to correct carbon dioxide and may decrease oxygen. His carbon dioxide is already raised as compensation. Tell: this is metabolic, and the fix is volume.

Correct. Vomiting (loss of hydrochloric acid) with orthostatic dizziness and a low urine chloride is saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, a sign of extracellular volume contraction. Isotonic saline corrects that volume deficit.

Bicarbonate is alkali; exogenous alkali is itself a cause of metabolic alkalosis and would push his pH of 7.51 higher. Isotonic saline treats the volume loss behind his alkalosis. Tell: adding alkali to an alkalemia raises the pH further.

D.q: A 61-year-old man who smokes has coughed up thick sputum most days for 4 months of each of the last 3 years. He has rhonchi, bluish lips and swelling of both ankles. His blood gas shows low oxygen and raised carbon dioxide, and his diffusing capacity is near normal. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows a ratio of 0.64. Which subtype best describes his disease?
opts: Chronic bronchitis without airflow obstruction is not this disease, but his ratio of 0.64 confirms obstruction. Tell: once the ratio is below 0.70, his chronic cough places him in the chronic bronchitis subtype.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Productive cough for at least 3 months a year over 2 years, rhonchi, cyanosis, edema, early hypoxemia and hypercapnia, and a near-normal diffusing capacity, with confirmed obstruction (ratio 0.64), are the chronic bronchitis picture (the blue bloater).

Emphysema brings a thin, pursed-lip breather with preserved gas exchange until late and a reduced diffusing capacity. He has early hypoxemia and hypercapnia with a near-normal diffusing capacity. Tell: sputum, cyanosis and edema point to bronchitis.
ruled out by a stated finding

Asthma does not usually bring years of daily sputum, cyanosis, edema and chronic carbon dioxide retention in a smoker. Tell: his cough history meets the chronic bronchitis definition, with persistent obstruction.

D.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
D.q: Which flow-volume loop shape is typical of obstruction in this disease?
opts: Correct. The obstructive flow-volume loop has a scooped expiratory limb, because expiratory flow is limited by airway narrowing and loss of elastic recoil. Air trapping and hyperinflation follow.

Expiratory flow is limited by narrowing and lost recoil, so the expiratory limb cannot be normal. Tell: the hallmark is a scooped expiratory curve. A normal limb would argue against obstruction altogether.
ruled out by a stated finding
The limitation in this disease is expiratory, so the inspiratory limb is not the part that changes. Tell: look at the expiratory limb, which scoops inward.
Obstruction lowers expiratory flow; it does not raise the peak. Tell: the expiratory limb is scooped, reflecting airflow that falls off as the airways narrow and collapse.

D.q: What is the key to success in asthma treatment?
opts: Correct. The treatment goals are minimal chronic symptoms, no exacerbations or emergency visits, normal lung function and activity, and minimal drug side effects, and patient compliance is the key to reaching them. Non-compliance is also the most common reason for refractory symptoms.

Immunotherapy is an add-on for selected patients with allergic triggers, given in a controlled setting because it can induce bronchoconstriction. Compliance is named as the key to treatment success. Tell: a niche add-on cannot be the key for every patient.

A goal of asthma treatment is no limitation on physical activity, so avoiding activity runs against the plan. Exercise symptoms are prevented with medication instead. Tell: the goals list protects activity rather than restricting it.

Systemic corticosteroids are for exacerbations or refractory disease at the minimum dose, with side effects such as osteoporosis and ulcers; they are not the key to success. Compliance is. Tell: daily systemic steroids conflict with the goal of minimizing adverse effects.

D.q: A 66-year-old man with asthma had facial flushing, red eyes and wheezing several hours after taking aspirin last month. He now has low back pain from lifting. Which medication should he avoid?
opts: Celecoxib is a selective anti-inflammatory drug, which aspirin-sensitive patients may take, so it is not one he must avoid. Tell: his aspirin reaction rules out the non-selective group, of which ibuprofen is the common example.

Meloxicam is a selective anti-inflammatory drug, and selective agents may be used in aspirin-sensitive asthma. It is a safe pain option for this man. Tell: the agents he must avoid are the non-selective ones, such as ibuprofen and naproxen.

Correct. Flushing, conjunctival irritation and wheeze after aspirin, even when delayed up to 12 hours, mark aspirin-sensitive asthma. Ibuprofen is a non-selective anti-inflammatory drug that cross-reacts and must be avoided; selective agents may be used.

Albuterol is his short-acting rescue bronchodilator, which every patient with asthma needs; it relaxes airway smooth muscle and is not a trigger. Tell: the medications that worsen aspirin-sensitive asthma are aspirin and its non-selective relatives.

D.q: A 54-year-old woman who had a kidney transplant takes long-term prednisone and anti-rejection drugs. She has 10 days of progressive shortness of breath and a dry cough, and her chest radiograph shows diffuse bilateral perihilar infiltrates. Induced sputum microscopy and Pneumocystis molecular testing are negative, but suspicion remains high. Which test should be done next?
opts: Lactate dehydrogenase is nonspecific and cannot confirm Pneumocystis or establish treatment failure. Her problem is a negative specimen with high suspicion, which only a better respiratory sample can answer. Tell: a nonspecific blood marker cannot replace microbiologic confirmation.

Pulmonary function testing is not a routine acute diagnostic test for Pneumocystis, and a normal diffusing capacity cannot reliably exclude it. Tell: she needs organism confirmation from the lower airway, which lavage provides and a breathing test cannot.

Correct. A negative induced specimen does not exclude Pneumocystis, and bronchoalveolar lavage is considered when induced sputum is negative and suspicion remains high. Her transplant, steroid use and perihilar infiltrates keep suspicion high, and the lavage sample goes for microscopy or molecular testing and other infections.

Spontaneously expectorated sputum has poor sensitivity for Pneumocystis and should not be used to exclude the infection. After a negative induced sample, a weaker specimen adds nothing. Tell: the step after a negative induced sputum goes deeper, to lavage, not back to plain sputum.

D.q: A 44-year-old woman who moved to a high-altitude town months ago has a chronic respiratory alkalosis. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.47 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 27 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which serum electrolyte pattern accompanies her renal compensation?
opts: Correct. In respiratory alkalosis the kidneys excrete bicarbonate and retain chloride, giving a reduced bicarbonate, hyperchloremia and hypokalemia (cells also secrete hydrogen ions in exchange for potassium). Her bicarbonate of 19 shows that compensation.
Normal chloride with a high anion gap
A high gap with a normal chloride is the pattern of elevated-gap metabolic acidosis, a low pH disorder. Her pH is 7.47. Tell: the anion gap sorts metabolic acidosis, not respiratory alkalosis.
High potassium accompanies acidosis, and low chloride belongs to chronic respiratory acidosis. Her alkalosis lowers potassium and raises chloride. Tell: flip both values for a respiratory alkalosis.

Low chloride with a high bicarbonate is the compensation of chronic respiratory acidosis. Her bicarbonate is 19 and her carbon dioxide low. Tell: alkalosis compensation lowers bicarbonate and keeps chloride.

D.q: A 74-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has an exacerbation with marked breathlessness. Before attributing it to the exacerbation, his clinician wants to exclude acute heart failure. Which test is most useful for that purpose?
opts: An alpha-1 antitrypsin level diagnoses the deficiency in young, unexposed or basal-emphysema patients. Tell: it plays no role in excluding heart failure during an exacerbation.

Correct. Exacerbation evaluation includes oxygen saturation, a blood gas, a chest x-ray, an electrocardiogram, and B-type natriuretic peptide or troponin. B-type natriuretic peptide is the test for suspected associated heart failure, one of the diagnoses to exclude.
The 6-minute walk feeds the survival index in stable disease and is not an exacerbation test. Tell: heart failure is screened with B-type natriuretic peptide.
Spirometry confirms the diagnosis and grades airflow in stable disease. Tell: to exclude acute heart failure during an exacerbation, B-type natriuretic peptide is used.

D.q: A 30-year-old man has had mild asthma since childhood, controlled with occasional albuterol. He asks whether his asthma is likely to become severe as he ages. Which reply is most accurate?
opts: Severity rises steadily with each decade
Asthma severity rarely varies over a patient's life. Tell: the course is stable severity, with severe asthma usually severe at onset rather than built up over decades.

Correct. Asthma severity rarely varies for a given patient: mild asthma rarely becomes severe, and severe asthma is usually severe at onset. His long history of mild disease predicts it will most likely stay mild.
Most mild asthma turns severe within a decade
Severity rarely changes for a patient, so mild disease does not typically progress to severe. Tell: severe asthma is usually severe from the start, not a later stage of mild asthma.
Severe asthma is usually severe at onset, so it does not usually begin as mild disease. Tell: this reverses the course, in which a patient's severity stays largely the same from the start.

D.q: A 29-year-old woman who is 24 weeks pregnant has had 3 days of fever, myalgias and cough, and she is not short of breath. Influenza is strongly suspected, and a molecular test has been sent. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Baloxavir is not recommended in pregnancy, and its single-dose use is limited to uncomplicated influenza within 48 hours. She is pregnant and at day 3. Tell: both the pregnancy and the timing rule baloxavir out.
ruled out by a stated finding

Risk status supports prompt antiviral treatment even when symptoms began more than 48 hours ago, and pregnancy is a high-risk group. Tell: the 48-hour limit applies to baloxavir in uncomplicated cases, not to oseltamivir in a pregnant patient.

Clinical suspicion can justify treatment, and confirmation is not awaited in hospitalized, high-risk or progressively ill patients. Indicated antivirals are not withheld while results are pending. Tell: her pregnancy makes her high risk.

Correct. Pregnancy in any trimester is a high-risk group, and oseltamivir is preferred for high-risk patients, including in pregnancy. It is started promptly, even after 48 hours of symptoms, without waiting for confirmation in a high-risk patient.

D.q: A 52-year-old woman with acute bronchitis was managed with supportive care 10 days ago and at first improved. She now returns with a new temperature of 102.2°F, shortness of breath and crackles at the left base. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Correct. Worsening after initial improvement, fever and dyspnea are return precautions, and fever or focal findings prompt evaluation for pneumonia rather than empiric bronchitis antibiotics. A worsening cough means reconsidering the diagnosis, and suspected pneumonia is confirmed with chest radiography.

Fever or focal findings should prompt evaluation for pneumonia rather than empiric bronchitis antibiotics; an antibiotic without a diagnosis skips the step that decides the regimen. Tell: new crackles with fever call for imaging first.

Codeine combinations are avoided routinely for limited benefit and risks of sedation, respiratory depression and misuse, and they do nothing for a new fever with focal crackles. Tell: her problem is a possible new diagnosis, not cough control.

The 2 to 3 week cough applies to an uncomplicated course; improvement followed by worsening, new fever and dyspnea are return precautions that mean the course is no longer uncomplicated. Tell: reassurance fits a steady cough, not a relapse with fever.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.q: A 64-year-old woman has chronic cough, sputum, fatigue and weight loss. Computed tomography shows fibrocavitary disease, alternative diagnoses have been excluded, and her sputum cultures are negative, but one bronchoalveolar lavage culture grows Mycobacterium avium complex. Which best describes whether she meets the diagnostic criteria?
opts: Imaging is one domain; diagnosis requires compatible symptoms and imaging, excluded alternatives and microbiologic evidence. Tell: her criteria are met because the lavage culture supplies the microbiology, not because of the scan.
Not met; a biopsy is required

A qualifying biopsy is one route, not a requirement; a single positive bronchial wash or lavage can meet the microbiologic criterion. Tell: her lavage result is enough with her symptoms, imaging and excluded alternatives.

Correct. Nontuberculous lung disease requires all domains: compatible symptoms and imaging (fibrocavitary disease here), exclusion of alternatives, and microbiology. One positive bronchial wash or lavage can meet the microbiologic criterion, even when sputum is negative.
Not met; two sputum cultures needed

Two or more sputum cultures of the same species are the usual route, but one positive bronchial wash or lavage, or a qualifying biopsy, can also meet the microbiologic criterion. Tell: her lavage culture counts.

D.q: For at least how long is chronic cavitary histoplasmosis treated?
opts: A month echoes the old 4-week symptom rule, which the current guidance replaces. Tell: chronic cavitary disease needs azole therapy for at least 12 months.
Three months is far short of the course for chronic cavitary disease. Tell: the azole is given for at least 12 months.
Six months is half the needed course. Tell: chronic cavitary histoplasmosis needs at least 12 months of azole therapy.
Correct. Chronic cavitary disease requires prolonged azole therapy, usually at least 12 months. The current updates replace a simple 4-week symptom rule for deciding treatment.

D.q: A 71-year-old man with long-standing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a stable chronic respiratory acidosis. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 60 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 33 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which serum electrolyte finding is expected?
opts: An elevated gap marks a metabolic acidosis with added unmeasured anions; his disorder is respiratory, with a high bicarbonate. Tell: the gap is a tool for metabolic acidosis.

Correct. In chronic respiratory acidosis the kidneys excrete acid as ammonium chloride and retain bicarbonate, so hypochloremia accompanies the raised bicarbonate of 33. This is the renal compensation.

Hyperchloremia is the pattern of respiratory alkalosis compensation (kidneys retain chloride) and of normal-gap metabolic acidosis. His kidneys are excreting chloride. Tell: chronic respiratory acidosis is the low-chloride state.

His kidneys retain bicarbonate to offset the carbon dioxide; his is 33, high. A low bicarbonate marks metabolic acidosis or respiratory alkalosis compensation. Tell: the compensation for retained carbon dioxide is retained bicarbonate.

D.q: Alongside clinical judgment, which tool is preferred to support the admission decision in community-acquired pneumonia?
opts: Sputum cultures are selective, for severe disease or resistant-pathogen risk, and their results come too late to decide admission. Tell: the Pneumonia Severity Index plus judgment guides disposition.

Correct. The Pneumonia Severity Index plus clinical judgment is preferred for admission decisions; the five-item confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age score complements it but does not replace clinical judgment.

A white blood cell count alone does not set the place of care, and routine blood counts do not help every stable outpatient. Tell: the admission decision uses the Pneumonia Severity Index with judgment.
The chest radiograph confirms that pneumonia is present but is not the preferred admission tool. Tell: the place of care is chosen with the Pneumonia Severity Index plus judgment.

D.q: Which statement summarizes the hygiene hypothesis?
opts: Hand washing prevents viral asthma attacks

This is infection control, not the hygiene hypothesis. The hypothesis proposes that reduced childhood germ exposure may increase hypersensitivity. Tell: the hypothesis explains why asthma develops, not how to prevent an attack in someone who has it.
More childhood germ exposure causes asthma

The hypothesis runs the other way: germ exposure is thought to help the immune system develop, so less exposure, not more, may increase hypersensitivity. Tell: the hypothesis is named for hygiene, meaning too clean, not too dirty.
Antibiotic use in adulthood causes intrinsic asthma

Intrinsic asthma is non-atopic and of later onset, but it is not explained by adult antibiotic use. The hygiene hypothesis concerns reduced germ exposure in childhood. Tell: the hypothesis is about the developing immune system, so its window is childhood.
Less childhood germ exposure may increase hypersensitivity

Correct. The hygiene hypothesis holds that childhood exposure to germs helps the immune system develop, so decreased exposure may suppress that development and increase hypersensitivity. It remains controversial.

D.q: A 70-year-old unvaccinated man with diabetes and heart failure has mild coronavirus disease 2019 that began 6 days ago. His oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Systemic corticosteroids are not used for coronavirus disease 2019 without hypoxemia unless another indication exists. His saturation is 96% on room air. Tell: dexamethasone belongs to the hospital pathway for hypoxemia.

Molnupiravir is an adult alternative only when the preferred options are unsuitable, and remdesivir is still available within its 7-day window. Tell: the preferred option comes first when it is still possible.
Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir must start within 5 days of symptom onset, and he is at day 6. Tell: count the days; the 5-day window has closed, while the 7-day remdesivir window has not.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A high-risk outpatient with mild or moderate disease and no hypoxemia is offered nirmatrelvir/ritonavir within 5 days or a three-day intravenous remdesivir course within 7 days of symptom onset. At day 6 only the remdesivir window is still open, and his age, comorbidities and lack of vaccination make him high risk.
