E.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
E.q: A 70-year-old man with confirmed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a symptom assessment test score of 6 and a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 1. He had 2 moderate exacerbations treated at home in the past year. Under the current three-group scheme, which group is he in?
opts: Correct. Two moderate exacerbations in the past year make him high risk, and any high-risk patient is group E regardless of symptoms. His low symptom score of 6 does not change that; group E starts on a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic.
His symptoms (score 6, dyspnea grade 1) would fit group A, but 2 moderate exacerbations make him high risk. Tell: exacerbation risk overrides symptoms in the current scheme.
Few symptoms with high risk would be C in the 2020 four-group scheme. Tell: in the current scheme C and D merged into E, so 2 moderate exacerbations make him E whatever his symptoms.
Group B is low risk with more symptoms; he has few symptoms and high risk. Tell: 2 moderate exacerbations put him in E. B also requires more symptoms, and his score is 6.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
E.q: Which set of symptoms is typical of asthma?
opts: Constant fever, night sweats, and weight loss

Constant systemic symptoms such as fever, night sweats and weight loss are not asthma features and suggest infection or malignancy. Asthma is episodic wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness and cough. Tell: asthma comes and goes with triggers rather than producing steady systemic illness.
Pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward

Sharp chest pain relieved by leaning forward is a pericarditis pattern. Asthma presents with episodic wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness and cough. Tell: asthma patients may lean forward to breathe during an attack, but chest tightness, not positional pain, is the complaint.
Episodic wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness, and cough

Correct. Asthma symptoms vary but include episodic wheezing, dyspnea, chest tightness, cough and sputum production, occurring spontaneously or after a trigger and often worse at night. The episodic pattern reflects reversible obstruction.
Stridor that is loudest on inspiration

Inspiratory stridor points to an upper airway problem, such as vocal fold dysfunction or a laryngotracheal mass, which is in the differential. Asthma causes episodic expiratory wheezing, dyspnea and cough. Tell: asthma's noise is on expiration, not inspiration.

E.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
E.q: A 34-year-old man after a motor vehicle crash has a flail chest (a chest wall segment moving paradoxically) and shallow breathing. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.27 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 56 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 25 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which process explains this blood gas?
opts: Chronic respiratory acidosis would carry a bicarbonate raised about 3.5 per 10 mm Hg, near 30. His 25 shows the acute response to an injury hours old. Tell: an acute cause leaves bicarbonate near normal.
Hyperventilation would lower carbon dioxide and raise the pH. His carbon dioxide is 56 and his pH 7.27. Tell: pain-driven fast breathing causes respiratory alkalosis.

Correct. A high carbon dioxide of 56 matching a low pH, with a bicarbonate barely raised, is acute respiratory acidosis. Thoracic trauma, including flail chest and pneumothorax, is a listed acute cause.
Lactic acidosis is a metabolic acidosis with a low bicarbonate below 22. His is 25, normal, and the raised carbon dioxide drives the pH. Tell: metabolic acidosis shows in the bicarbonate.
ruled out by a stated finding
E.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 26

E.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
E.q: Which neuromuscular disorders are listed as causes of acute respiratory acidosis?
opts: Correct. Myasthenia gravis and Guillain-Barre syndrome are the listed neuromuscular causes of acute respiratory acidosis. Muscular dystrophy and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis are the neuromuscular causes of the chronic form.

Salicylates and nicotine are toxic causes of respiratory alkalosis. Myasthenia gravis and Guillain-Barre syndrome cause acute respiratory acidosis. Tell: toxins that stimulate breathing lead to alkalosis, not acidosis.
Muscular dystrophy and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

Muscular dystrophy and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis are the neuromuscular causes of chronic respiratory acidosis. The acute ones are myasthenia gravis and Guillain-Barre syndrome. Tell: acute and chronic have separate neuromuscular lists.

Pregnancy and hyperthyroidism are endocrine causes of respiratory alkalosis. The acute neuromuscular causes of respiratory acidosis are myasthenia gravis and Guillain-Barre syndrome. Tell: the stem asks for neuromuscular disorders, and these are endocrine.
E.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 26

E.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
E.q: A 45-year-old man with Guillain-Barré syndrome has worsening weakness and shallow breathing. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.26 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 58 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 26 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is the priority treatment for his acid-base disorder?
opts: Renal compensation begins only after 6 to 12 hours, takes days, and never returns the pH to normal. His breathing is failing now. Tell: compensation alone never restores the pH; the disorder must be corrected.

Careful oxygen titration is the approach for chronic respiratory acidosis. His is acute (bicarbonate 26), and the priority is restoring ventilation. Tell: acute equals restore ventilation; chronic equals careful oxygen.

Correct. A high carbon dioxide with a low pH and a barely raised bicarbonate is acute respiratory acidosis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome is a listed neuromuscular cause. Acute respiratory acidosis is treated by restoring ventilation while the cause is treated.
Give sodium bicarbonate to raise the pH

His acidosis comes from retained carbon dioxide, so the fix is ventilation; therapy aimed at the pH itself is reserved for an unsustainable pH (below 6.7), alongside the cause. His pH is 7.26. Tell: respiratory acidosis is treated by breathing, not by bicarbonate.
E.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 28

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
E.q: A 45-year-old man with human immunodeficiency virus infection has mild Pneumocystis pneumonia. He had a severe rash with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in the past, so clindamycin plus primaquine is planned. Which test should be checked before primaquine is given?
opts: Beta-D-glucan is a diagnostic marker, where a low result makes Pneumocystis less likely; it is not organism-specific and says nothing about drug safety. His diagnosis is already made. Tell: the question is about the drug, not the diagnosis.

Lactate dehydrogenase is nonspecific: it cannot confirm Pneumocystis or establish treatment failure, and it is not a safety check for any drug. Tell: the pre-primaquine test is an enzyme deficiency screen, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.

Correct. His past reaction removes trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and clindamycin plus primaquine is a severity-based alternative. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is checked before primaquine or dapsone, because a deficiency makes those drugs unsafe.

Pulmonary function testing is not a routine acute test in Pneumocystis pneumonia, and it does not screen for primaquine safety. Tell: before primaquine or dapsone, the required check is glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
E.q: A 63-year-old woman develops ventilator-associated pneumonia on day 5 of mechanical ventilation and is in septic shock, which places her at high mortality risk. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is common in her unit. Which empiric regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. High mortality risk and local methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus prevalence add vancomycin or linezolid to an antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as cefepime; a second antipseudomonal class may be used for selected high-risk patients. Cultures are obtained, therapy reassessed daily and de-escalated.

Cefepime by itself fits hospital or ventilator pneumonia without major resistance or high mortality risk. Her septic shock and the unit's methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus prevalence call for added vancomycin or linezolid. Tell: high risk adds coverage.

Linezolid covers methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, but moxifloxacin is not a reliable antipseudomonal agent, which leaves her most likely organisms uncovered. Tell: pair the staphylococcal agent with cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam.

This is a community-acquired pneumonia regimen. Ventilator-associated pneumonia is more likely Pseudomonas or multidrug-resistant organisms. Tell: the ventilator pathway uses an antipseudomonal beta-lactam, not ceftriaxone.

E.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
E.q: A 68-year-old woman going home on oxygen asks what signs to post. Which signage is taught?
opts: A sign with her recertification date

Her recertification date is not a posted sign. Recertification is about keeping home oxygen qualified at 12 or 3 months, whereas signs are about safety in the home. Tell: dates belong in her chart; warnings belong on the wall.
A sign with her oxygen flow rate

A sign with her oxygen flow rate is not part of the signage taught. The taught signs warn about smoking and oxygen use because of the fire hazard. Tell: signs are for warning others, not for recording her prescription.
A sign with her pharmacy's number
The pharmacy's number is not part of the signage taught. The signs are No Smoking and, potentially, Oxygen in Use. Tell: signage addresses the fire hazard, not contact information.
No Smoking and Oxygen in Use signs

Correct. Home oxygen teaching is to post No Smoking signage, and potentially Oxygen in Use signs, within the home. Oxygen is highly flammable, and the signs warn everyone who enters, including visitors and firefighters.

E.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
E.q: A 41-year-old man with asthma is reviewing his written action plan with you. Which finding is a danger sign telling him to take his quick-relief medicine and go to the hospital or call an ambulance now?
opts: Mild wheeze with the first signs of a cold
The first signs of a cold and mild wheeze are caution, or yellow-zone, features. Tell: those call for adding quick-relief medicine, while blue lips or fingernails call for the hospital now.
Peak flow at 75% of personal best

A reading of 75% of personal best falls in the yellow zone, 50% to 79%. Tell: the red zone starts below 50%, and the danger signs are blue lips or fingernails and trouble walking and talking from breathlessness.

Night cough, like waking at night with asthma, is a yellow-zone sign that asthma is getting worse. Tell: yellow means add quick-relief medicine and keep the controller; the danger signs are blue lips or trouble walking and talking.

Correct. The action plan's danger signs are trouble walking and talking because of shortness of breath, and lips or fingernails that are blue. Either one means take the quick-relief medicine and go to the hospital or call an ambulance now, without waiting.

E.topic: Reading the fraction from the flow
E.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
E.q: A 75-year-old man's family turned his home nasal cannula up to 9 L/min because he felt short of breath. About what fraction of inspired oxygen does he receive at that setting?
opts: Correct. A nasal cannula can be turned to any setting, but the fraction stops at 44% (reached at 6 L/min). At 9 L/min he gets no more than that, so the extra 3 liters add oxygen to his nose but not to his fraction.

56% would follow from continuing to add 4% per liter, but the cannula's fraction maxes out at 44%. The knob can turn over 6 L/min, yet the fraction does not rise. Tell: the cannula has a ceiling; the arithmetic stops at 6 L/min.
60% belongs to the low end of a non-rebreather mask's 60-100% range at 10-15 L/min. A cannula does not reach it. Tell: you need a reservoir bag device to get above 44%.
100% is the top of the non-rebreather's range, requiring a reservoir bag and 10-15 L/min. A cannula at 9 L/min cannot reach it. Tell: the cannula is a low flow device with a hard ceiling of 44%.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
E.q: A 69-year-old woman is diagnosed with Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease. Her husband asks whether he needs testing because she is contagious, as with tuberculosis. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Correct. Most nontuberculous mycobacterial infections arise from environmental exposure, and person-to-person spread is uncommon. That is one reason species identification matters: transmission differs between nontuberculous mycobacteria and the tuberculosis complex.
She is contagious until treatment ends

Being contagious until cleared is a tuberculosis idea, and even there isolation ends by clinical, laboratory and public-health criteria. Tell: her nontuberculous infection came from the environment, and spread between people is uncommon.
He needs airborne precautions at home
Airborne precautions are for pulmonary or laryngeal tuberculosis. Tell: her organism is an environmental nontuberculous species that rarely spreads between people.
He needs a tuberculin skin test now
Testing after exposure is a step for contacts of infectious tuberculosis. Tell: Mycobacterium avium complex is not in the tuberculosis complex and comes mostly from the environment.

E.io: Define, describe, and discuss aspergillosis as it relates to asthma.
E.q: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis occurs almost exclusively in patients with which conditions?
opts: Correct. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, a hypersensitivity to Aspergillus fumigatus, occurs almost exclusively with asthma or cystic fibrosis, and it presents as acute asthma symptoms or an exacerbation.
Heart failure causes cardiac asthma, a mimic; it is not the setting for this hypersensitivity, which is asthma or cystic fibrosis. Tell: the hosts are airway diseases, not heart diseases.

Acute infections are not the setting. The reaction occurs almost exclusively in asthma or cystic fibrosis, two chronic airway diseases. Tell: the host conditions are lifelong airway disorders, not short-lived infections.

Neither is the host condition, although obesity makes asthma harder to control. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis occurs almost exclusively in asthma or cystic fibrosis. Tell: the reaction needs an already diseased airway, not a metabolic condition.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
E.q: Why can a mycobacterial culture take weeks to return a result?
opts: Smear conversion is not a precondition for reading a culture; the smear and the culture are requested together on each specimen. Tell: the delay belongs to the slow-growing organism, not to any other test.

Correct. Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows slowly, so cultures can take weeks. That is why a rapid molecular test is run on at least one respiratory specimen alongside the smear and culture: molecular tests can give results quickly.

Molecular tests run alongside the culture, not before it, and they are the fast part of the workup. The culture is slow because of the organism. Tell: molecular tests are the rapid result, culture is the slow one.
The three sputum specimens are collected 8 to 24 hours apart and each is sent for smear and culture; they are not pooled. Tell: the weeks come from slow growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
E.cite: 38. Mycobacterial Infections including Tuberculosis - Bobilin - 10-29-2025 SV.pptx, Slide 4

E.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
E.q: A 64-year-old woman completes the 8-item symptom assessment test, each item scored 0 to 5: cough 2, phlegm 1, chest tightness 1, breathlessness on a hill or flight of stairs 3, limitation of home activities 2, confidence leaving home 1, sleep 1, and energy 2. What is her total score?
opts: Eleven drops 2 points, as if the energy item (2) were left out. Tell: all 8 items count, so add energy back: 11 + 2 = 13. Either way, her total of 13 is above the line of 10.
Twelve misses 1 point, as if one of the 1-point items (phlegm, chest tightness, confidence or sleep) were skipped. Tell: there are four 1-point items, and all of them count.

Correct. Cough 2 + phlegm 1 + chest tightness 1 + breathlessness on stairs 3 + home activities 2 + confidence leaving home 1 + sleep 1 + energy 2 = 13. A total of 10 or more counts as more symptoms when assigning her group.

Fourteen adds a point that is not there, as if breathlessness on stairs were scored 4 instead of 3. Tell: recheck each item; the correct sum is 13. An extra point would not change her group, but it is not the sum.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
E.q: A 69-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease had 2 moderate exacerbations and 1 hospital admission in the past year. His blood eosinophil count is 350. He is starting maintenance therapy. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: An inhaled corticosteroid is never used alone in this disease; it must be combined with a long-acting beta agonist. Tell: his eosinophils justify adding it to dual bronchodilators, not using it by itself.
Oral corticosteroids are for acute exacerbations only, not maintenance. Tell: frequent exacerbations are prevented with inhaled long-acting therapy, here triple therapy because of his eosinophils.

Correct. Two moderate exacerbations and an admission make him high risk, group E. Group E starts on a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic, and adding an inhaled corticosteroid is considered when blood eosinophils are 300 or more, as his 350 are.

A single bronchodilator is the group A start, for few symptoms and low risk. His exacerbations and admission make him group E. Tell: high risk calls for both long-acting bronchodilators, plus a steroid with eosinophils of 300 or more.

E.io: Identify compensatory mechanisms for simple acid-base disorders.
E.q: A 66-year-old man has had respiratory acidosis for several days, and his carbon dioxide is 60 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg). Using bicarbonate rises of about 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg acutely and about 3.5 per 10 chronically, from a midpoint of 24, which bicarbonate fits chronic compensation?
opts: 24 assumes no compensation at all. After several days the kidneys have retained bicarbonate, to about 31. Tell: a respiratory problem that lasts days shows a rise in bicarbonate.
ruled out by a stated finding
26 is the acute response, 1 per 10 mm Hg (24 + 2). Several days in, the chronic response is about 24 + 7 = 31. Tell: the stem gives the time course, and several days means chronic.

Correct. Carbon dioxide rose 20 mm Hg (40 to 60). Chronically bicarbonate rises about 3.5 per 10 mm Hg, so 24 + 7 = 31; acutely it would be only 24 + 2 = 26. Renal compensation takes days to complete, and he has had several days.
38 overshoots; it would need about 7 per 10 mm Hg. The chronic ratio of 3.5 per 10 gives 24 + 7 = 31. Tell: apply 3.5 to the 20 mm Hg rise, which is two steps of 10.

Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
E.q: A 63-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and a past opioid use disorder has acute bronchitis. His oxygen saturation and vital signs are normal. He asks for a codeine cough syrup that helped a friend. Which treatment should be avoided?
opts: A short bronchodilator trial may help selected patients with wheeze or airflow obstruction, and his chronic obstructive pulmonary disease makes that reasonable if he wheezes, with reassessment. Tell: a bronchodilator opens the airways; the opioid suppressant is the one that depresses breathing.

Acetaminophen is a reasonable comfort measure for fever or discomfort in acute bronchitis; the caution with it is duplicate dosing from combination products. Tell: the drug to avoid here is the one that sedates, depresses breathing and can be misused, which acetaminophen does not.

Rest, hydration and avoiding smoke or other irritants may improve comfort and carry no special risk for him. Tell: these are the expected-course comfort measures; the codeine product is the one with sedation, respiratory depression and misuse risks.

Correct. Routine opioid cough suppressants are avoided: codeine-containing combinations have limited benefit and carry sedation, respiratory depression and misuse risks. His lung disease raises the stakes of respiratory depression, and his opioid use disorder raises the misuse risk.

E.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
E.q: A 58-year-old woman with asthma and nasal polyps developed wheezing, facial flushing and a runny nose within an hour of taking aspirin last year. She now has painful knee osteoarthritis and asks for an anti-inflammatory pain reliever. Which drug is the most appropriate choice?
opts: Naproxen is a non-selective anti-inflammatory drug, and patients with aspirin-sensitive asthma cross-react with that group. Her past aspirin reaction rules it out. Tell: the safe choices for her are the selective agents, celecoxib and meloxicam.

Correct. Her wheeze, flushing and rhinorrhea after aspirin mark aspirin-sensitive asthma, so non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs must be avoided. Selective agents such as celecoxib or meloxicam may be used, which treats her knee pain without the cross-reaction.

Diclofenac is on the list of non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs to avoid in aspirin-sensitive asthma, and her flushing and wheeze after aspirin show that sensitivity. Tell: selective agents such as celecoxib are the ones she may use.

Indomethacin is a non-selective anti-inflammatory drug, the group that worsens aspirin-sensitive asthma, so her aspirin reaction rules it out. Tell: only the selective agents (celecoxib, meloxicam) are allowed in aspirin-sensitive asthma.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
E.q: A 32-year-old woman with no medical conditions has community-acquired pneumonia and is stable for outpatient treatment. She has no risk for resistant organisms, and local pneumococcal resistance to macrolides is 30%. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
opts: A beta-lactam such as cefpodoxime plus azithromycin is the regimen for outpatients with comorbidities such as chronic heart, lung, liver or renal disease, diabetes, alcoholism, malignancy or asplenia. She has none. Tell: combination therapy is for comorbid patients.

Macrolide monotherapy is used only if local pneumococcal resistance is below 25%. At 30% resistance azithromycin by itself is not appropriate. Tell: the resistance figure in the stem is the decisive clue against the macrolide.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. With no comorbidities and no resistant-organism risk, the outpatient choices are amoxicillin or doxycycline. Macrolide monotherapy is used only if local pneumococcal resistance is below 25%, and hers is 30%, so amoxicillin fits.

A respiratory fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin is an outpatient option for patients with comorbidities, with its QT, interaction and fluoroquinolone risks reviewed. She has no comorbidities. Tell: healthy outpatients get amoxicillin or doxycycline first.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for respiratory infections in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
E.q: Which group is at high risk for severe influenza?
opts: Age 50 to 64 without disease is not a high-risk group for severe influenza. Tell: the age-based risk starts at 65 in adults.
Recent travel or animal exposure can change testing and public health needs, but it is not itself a severe-disease risk category. Tell: age 65 or older is.

Correct. High-risk groups include adults 65 or older, children younger than 5 (especially younger than 2), residents of long-term care facilities, immunocompromised patients, pregnancy and the first 2 weeks postpartum, severe obesity and chronic organ disease.
Healthy school-age children are not listed; the pediatric high-risk group is children younger than 5, especially younger than 2. Tell: risk sits at the extremes of age.

E.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
E.q: A 33-year-old woman at 30 weeks of pregnancy has a routine arterial blood gas for mild breathlessness: pH 7.46 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 28 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: Acute compensation lowers bicarbonate only about 2 per 10 mm Hg, to about 22 (12 below 40). Her 19 shows the fuller chronic response. Tell: pregnancy is a sustained state, so the kidneys have had time.

Correct. The pH of 7.46 is alkalemia, and the carbon dioxide of 28 is low and matches it: respiratory alkalosis. Bicarbonate fell about 5 per 10 mm Hg (12 below 40 gives about 18 to 19), a chronic renal response. Pregnancy is a listed endocrine cause.
Respiratory acidosis is a high carbon dioxide with a low pH. She has a low carbon dioxide of 28 and a high pH of 7.46. Tell: both values point the opposite way.

Her bicarbonate is low, but her pH of 7.46 is high, so this is not an acidosis. The low bicarbonate is compensation for the respiratory alkalosis. Tell: the pH direction identifies the primary disorder.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
E.q: A 52-year-old man has 12 mm of induration on a tuberculin skin test. His chest radiograph shows a fibrotic upper-lobe lesion, he does not recall ever being treated for tuberculosis, and he has no symptoms. Which step must come before latent-infection treatment?
opts: The blood test shows infection, which his skin test already shows, and neither test distinguishes latent infection from disease. Tell: the missing step is excluding active disease.

Correct. Fibrotic lesions warrant review of prior treatment and exclusion of active disease, and tuberculosis disease must be excluded before latent-infection treatment begins. Imaging cannot reliably determine activity, so microbiologic testing answers that question.
A repeat skin test in 8 to 10 weeks

Repeat testing 8 to 10 weeks after exposure is for an early negative result after a recent exposure. Tell: his test is already positive, and his lesion raises the question of active disease, which must be excluded.
A second chest radiograph in 1 year

Waiting a year leaves possible active disease unaddressed; fibrotic lesions warrant exclusion of active disease now. Tell: imaging cannot reliably determine activity, so microbiology is needed before treatment.

E.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
E.q: A patient meets the clinical definition of chronic bronchitis, but spirometry shows no airflow obstruction. How is this classified?
opts: Correct. Chronic bronchitis without airflow obstruction is not chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The diagnosis requires obstruction confirmed by spirometry, a post-bronchodilator ratio of the 1-second volume to forced vital capacity below 0.70.
The chronic bronchitis subtype of the disease still requires persistent airflow obstruction. Tell: cough and sputum alone, with normal spirometry, fall outside the disease entirely.
Emphysema is defined by alveolar destruction and enlargement, and it also causes obstruction. Tell: this patient has symptoms of chronic bronchitis and no obstruction, so neither subtype applies.

Grade 1 (mild) describes a patient who already has the disease, with a ratio below 0.70 and a 1-second volume of 80% predicted or more. Tell: grading starts only after obstruction is confirmed, and this patient has none.

E.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
E.q: A 70-year-old woman with cirrhosis and an albumin of 1.9 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.0 g/dL) has a metabolic acidosis, a chloride of 110 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L) and an anion gap of 11 (normal 9 to 15). Which finding most limits how much the normal gap can reassure you?
opts: Losing unmeasured cations (calcium, magnesium, potassium) raises the gap, so it would make a normal value less likely, not falsely reassuring. Her low albumin lowers it. Tell: fewer cations raise the gap; less albumin lowers it.

Correct. Albumin accounts for most of the normal anion gap, so hypoalbuminemia lowers the gap and can hide added unmeasured anions. A normal gap does not exclude a high-gap acidosis and should not override clinical concern.

A high chloride marks a true normal-gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis; it is a finding, not an error in the gap. Her low albumin is the listed source of error. Tell: hypoalbuminemia sits on the error list; chloride does not.

The acidosis is what the gap is meant to sort; it does not distort the number. Hypoalbuminemia does, by removing the anion that makes up most of the normal gap. Tell: look for the listed errors: low albumin, sodium extremes, antibiotics.

E.io: Identify and discuss vaccines which prevent respiratory infections.
E.q: A 32-year-old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant received Tdap during her last pregnancy 2 years ago. Which plan for pertussis protection is appropriate?
opts: Td lacks the pertussis component, and Tdap is what protects against pertussis. The recommendation is Tdap during every pregnancy. Tell: pertussis protection needs the Tdap product.
Wait 10 years from her last Tdap
The 10-year Td or Tdap booster interval applies to adults outside pregnancy. Tdap is given during every pregnancy. Tell: pregnancy resets the clock; each pregnancy gets its own dose.
The recommendation is Tdap during every pregnancy, not after delivery. Tell: the dose belongs in the pregnancy itself.
Correct. Tdap is given during every pregnancy, regardless of the interval since the last dose. Her dose 2 years ago in an earlier pregnancy does not cover this one, so she receives Tdap now.

E.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
E.q: A 68-year-old woman with diabetes and an acute myocardial infarction has an oxygen saturation of 87% on room air. Which is the right approach to oxygen?
opts: Withhold oxygen because of her diabetes

Diabetes is not a listed reason to withhold oxygen. The hazards listed are carbon dioxide retention, fire, mucosal irritation and vasoconstriction, and the myocardial infarction rule turns on a saturation under 91%. Tell: the saturation decides, not her comorbidity.
Wait for an arterial blood gas first

An arterial blood gas is not required before treating. A pulse oximeter reading of 87% already shows she is below 91%, and delaying oxygen leaves hypoxia uncorrected. Tell: the threshold rests on the saturation she already has; no extra test is needed to start.

Vasoconstriction is the reason oxygen is withheld in a myocardial infarction, but that applies unless the saturation is below 91%. At 87% she is below it, so the exception applies. Tell: withhold when the saturation is 91% or higher, give when it is below 91%.
Give oxygen, since saturation is below 91%

Correct. Her saturation of 87% is below the 91% cutoff. Oxygen is held back in a myocardial infarction because of vasoconstriction, but only while the saturation is 91% or higher. She is hypoxic, so the benefit of correcting hypoxia wins and she should receive oxygen.
